نظامِ تعلیم ہماری سب سے اہم ترجیحات میں شامل ہونا چاہیے۔ محترم استاد! آپ کا گلگت کی قانون ساز اسمبلی کا رکن بننا تعلیم سے وابستہ ہر شخص کے لیے یقیناً خوش آئند ہے۔ آپ نے برسوں درس و تدریس کے میدان میں خدمات انجام دی ہیں، اس لیے آپ سے یہ توقع اور بھی بڑھ جاتی ہے کہ اب اسمبلی کے اندر بھی تعلیم کے حق میں ایک مؤثر اور توانا آواز بنیں گے۔ گلگت بلتستان کے لاکھوں بچوں کا مستقبل اس بات سے جڑا ہے کہ انہیں کس معیار کی تعلیم، کس ماحول اور کن مواقع تک رسائی حاصل ہوتی ہے۔ ایک ایسا سرکاری نظامِ تعلیم ضروری ہے جہاں امیر اور غریب کے بچے کے لیے تعلیم کا معیار مختلف نہ ہو، شہر اور دور دراز علاقوں کے بچوں کے مواقع مختلف نہ ہوں، اور کسی بچے کا مستقبل اس کی مالی حیثیت کا محتاج نہ ہو۔ گلگت کی 25 لاکھ آبادی ایک ایسے سرکاری نظامِ تعلیم کی مستحق ہے جو مساوات، معیار اور مواقع کی برابری پر قائم ہو۔ بعض لوگ یہ سوال اٹھا سکتے ہیں کہ گلگت کا سیاسی اور سماجی خد و خال کم و بیش وہی ہے جو پاکستان کے دوسرے حصوں کا ہے اور یہ نظامِ تعلیم لگ بھگ ناممکن سا خواب ہے۔ اگر تعلیم پر سیاست نہ کی جائےاور سنجیدہ کوشش کی جائے تو یہ خواب حقیقت بن سکتا ہے۔ دنیا بھر میں اس طرح کی کئی مثالیں موجود ہیں۔ فن لینڈ میں سارے اسکول ایک جیسے ہیں، جبکہ سری لنکا میں 1980 کی دہائی کے بعد کوئی نیا پرائیویٹ اسکول کھولنے کی اجازت ہی نہیں دی گئی ہے۔ دوسری جانب، گلگت کی ہر گلی میں اتنے پرائیویٹ اسکول ہیں کہ یونیفارم کے لیے کپڑوں کے ر نگ کم پڑ گئے ہیں۔ اخر کیوں گورنمنٹ نے ہر ایک کو اسکول کھلنے اجازت دی ہے اور ان اسکولوں میں تعلیمی معیار کو کس طرح یقینی بنایا جاتا ہے؟ لو کوسٹ(low cost) اور سرکاری اسکولوں میں پڑھائی جانے والی کتابیں آج بھی وہی ہیں جو کئی دہائیاں پہلے ہمارے والدین نے پڑھی تھیں۔ پڑھائے جانے والے قومی نصاب میں گلگت کی ثقافت اور زبانوں کے لیے کوئی جگہ نہیں، اور نہ گلگتی عوام کی بنیادی حقوق کی بات ہوتی ہیں۔ توجہ صرف اس بات پر مرکوز ہے کہ بچہ کسی طرح امتحان میں پاس ہوجائے۔ ۔ہاں البتہ الیٹ(elite) پرائیویٹ اسکولز جو چاہیں وہ بڑھا سکتے ہیں۔ کچھ پرائیویٹ اسکول اچھا کام بھی کر رہے ہوں گے، لیکن میں ان کو کاروبار کہوں گا۔ یہ اسکول کم تنخواہوں پر اساتذہ کی بھرتی اور معیاری تعلیم کے نام پر بھاری بھرکم فیس وصول کرتے ہیں۔ استاد جی، اگر گلگت کے تعلیمی نظام میں اصلاح کرنا ہے تو سب سے پہلے”نو مور پرائیویٹ اسکول“ کہنا ہوگا اور اس کاروبار کو مکمل بند کرنے کی ہمت کرنی ہوگی۔ اگر سرکار مفت تعلیم نہیں دے سکتی تو آئین سے آرٹیکل 25-اے کو ہمیشہ ہمیشہ کے لیے ختم کر دینا چاہیے تاکہ جس کی جیسی مرضی، اپنے لیے تعلیم حاصل کر سکے۔ دوسری چیز اساتذہ کی تعلیم اور ٹریننگ ہے۔ اس میں دو چیزیں کرنے کی اشد ضرورت ہے۔ قراقرم انٹرنیشنل یونیورسٹی کے ایجوکیشن ڈیپارٹمنٹ کو ٹیچرز ٹریننگ انسٹیٹیوٹ کا درجہ دیا جائے اور بی ایڈ(B.ED)سمیت تمام ڈپلومےختم کیے جائیں۔ ۔بی ایڈ ایک درآمد شدہ ڈگری ہے جو مجھے اپنے مطلوبہ مقاصد کے حصول میں کامیاب نظر نہیں اتی۔ وجہ یہ ہے کہ اس میں کنٹینٹ نالج(content knowledge) پر کم اور زیادہ توجہ پیڈاگوجی(pedagogy) پر دیا جاتا ہے۔ اخر میں اساتذہ کو یہ تو معلوم ہوتا ہے کہ کس طرح پڑھانا ہے، لیکن پڑھانے کے لیے کنٹینٹ نالج ہی نہیں ہوتا۔ اس مسئلے کا حل یہ ہے کہ ٹیچرز کے لیے پانچ سالہ ماسٹرز کی ڈگری تشکیل دی جائے۔ پورے گلگت میں بارہویں جماعت کے طلبہ سے امتحان لیا جائے اور انٹرویو میں سوال کیا جائے کہ وہ کیوں ٹیچرز بننا چاہتے ہیں۔ تسلی کے بعد 100 بہترین طلبہ کو پانچ سال کی مفت تعلیم دی جائے۔ شروع کے تین سال کنٹینٹ، پیڈاگوجی، آرٹس، اے آئی، اسپورٹس، زبانوں اور ایڈمنسٹریشن کے کورسز پڑھائے جائیں۔ اور آخری دو سال میں معیاری ریسرچ کرائی جائے تاکہ ٹیچرز پیئر ریویو جرنلز (peer reviewed journals) میں پیپرز شائع کر سکیں۔ ساتھ ہی ڈگری کے دوران سرکاری اور پرائیویٹ اسکولوں میں سپروائزر(supervisor) کی نگرانی میں پریکٹیکم(practicum) کے ذریعے ٹیچر سے توقعات، ایڈمنسٹریشن اور بچوں کو سمجھنے کی عملی تربیت دی جائے۔ تعلیم مکمل ہونے کے بعدان ٹیچرز کی تعیناتی کے وقت یہ ذمہ داری دیا جائے کہ اپنے اسکول کو ایک مثالی اسکول بنائیں۔ اب اسکول میں ٹیچرز تو آ گئے ہیں، لیکن اس کے بعد کمیونٹی انگیجمنٹ(commmunity engagement) اور وسائل(resourses) کی بروقت فراہمی بھی ضروری بنائی جائے۔ اگلا سوال یہ ہے کہ اسکول میں کیا پڑھایا جائے؟ اس کامکمل جواب پھر کبھی۔ مختصراً یہ کہ وہی جو وقت کا تقاضا ہے اور ساتھ میں ہمیں اپنے ماضی کے بارے میں پتہ ہونا چاہیے، جو ہمیں حال میں رہنے کے قابل بنائے اور کل کے تمام سیاسی، سماجی اور موسمیاتی مسائل کو حل کرنے کے لیے تیار کر سکے۔ اور اگر ابھی تیار نہ ہو سکے تو موسمیاتی تبدیلی اور خطے کے سیاسی صورتحال کی وجہ سےشاید گلگت کل رہائش کے قابل ہی نہیں رہے گا۔۔۔

description_en: A Physics lesson on time dilation, exploring the relativity of time through the twin paradox and Einstein's theory of relativity.
description_ur: زمانی تمدد (ٹائم ڈائی لیشن) پر فزکس کا سبق، جڑواں تضاد اور آئن سٹائن کے نظریۂ اضافیت کے ذریعے وقت کی اضافیت کا جائزہ۔
content: Grade B.Ed-VIII Duration 15 Minutes Subject Physics Class strength 16 Topic Time Dilation 1. Student Learning Objectives Students will be able to: I. Understand that time is relative. II. Apply the concept of time dilation in different scenarios. 2. Required Material Whiteboard, duster, markers or chalk, ruler, computer, projector, a ball 3. Motivation Activity (2 Minutes) Begin by asking the students to reflect on the concept of time. Pose questions like: What is time for you? How do you perceive time? Do you think time is constant? 4. Introductory Activity (3 Minutes) Introduce the twin paradox as a thought experiment to illustrate time dilation. Explain the scenario where one twin travels at near the speed of light while the other stays on Earth. Discuss how this leads to a difference in aging between the twins. 5. Activity 2 (6 Minutes) Define time dilation as the difference in elapsed time measured by two observers due to a relative difference in velocity or gravitational potential between them. Explain the basics of Einstein's theory of relativity and how it challenges our traditional understanding of time. Use a diagram and derived equation of time dilation, showing how time can pass differently for observers in different reference frames. 6. Assessment Activity (4 Minutes) Evaluate students' understanding by asking them to explain the concept of time dilation and its potential uses. 7. description_en: An English lesson on revisiting free writing, using Communicative Language Teaching with a constructivist approach and the 5E model.
description_ur: آزاد تحریر کے دوبارہ جائزے پر انگریزی کا سبق، ابلاغی زبان کی تدریس، تعمیری انداز اور 5E ماڈل کے ذریعے۔
content: Grade VII Duration 40 Minutes Subject English Class strength 48 Topic Revisiting Free Writing Philosophy: Constructivism    Approach: Student Centered    Method: Communicative Language Teaching 1. Students' Learning Outcomes Students will be able to: R U A A E C Total I. Revise and enhance free writing composition to improve communication. - - 50% - - - 50% II. Demonstrate the ability to present and express original ideas independently by freewriting. - - 50% - - - 50% Total 100% R = remembering, U = understanding, A = applying, A = analysing, E = evaluating, C = creating 2. Pedagogy Learning Outcome Students would have a better understanding of free writing as a tool for self-expression and creativity. 3. Required Material Whiteboard and Marker Duster 4. 5E Plan Engagement Start the course with a quick review of the previous class on free writing. Ask students to share their thoughts on the concept of free writing based on the previous lesson Exploration Remind students of the definition of freelance writing and its benefits. Introduce additional incentives for free writing and encourage students to explore different texts or topics. Example: Describe a moment that changed your mind or write a conversation between two people with opposing viewpoints. Explanation Facilitate class discussion about the value of sharing and receiving feedback Incorporate the idea of revision and discipline into your writing. Discuss specific areas of writing that could be improved, such as word choice, sentence structure, and clarity of explanation. Based on the comments, model the process of modifying the text. Elaboration Have students review an earlier text for free or use one of the new prompts. In pairs or small groups, students edit their writing and provide constructive feedback. Encourage students to focus on specific aspects of the text discussed in class, such as adding emotional detail, using sentence structure, etc. Evaluation Ask each student to reflect on the information they have received and the process of making changes to their writing. Facilitate class discussion of her challenges and successes. 5. Assessment Matrix SLOs Method Type Tool Strategy I Inductive Subjective --- --- II Deductive Subjective Exit Ticket writing 6. description_en: What a practicum is, and why this diary of lesson plans, reflections, and reflective reports is being published.
description_ur: پریکٹیکم کیا ہوتا ہے، اور سبقی منصوبوں، تاثرات اور تفکراتی رپورٹس پر مشتمل یہ ڈائری کیوں شائع کی جا رہی ہے۔
content: A practicum is a period of supervised teaching practice built into a B.Ed. (Bachelor of Education) degree. Rather than only studying theories of teaching, student teachers spend time in real classrooms: observing experienced teachers, planning and delivering their own lessons, receiving feedback from supervisors and peers, and writing reflections on what happened and what they would do differently next time. Over the course of a degree, several practicums build on one another, moving from short observation visits toward longer, more independent stretches of teaching. This diary collects the lesson plans, reflections, and reflective reports I wrote across five practicums between 2021 and 2024, while training to become a teacher. I'm publishing it as an honest record of that process, mistakes and all, in the hope that it's useful to other student teachers, to the teachers who supervised and taught alongside me, and to anyone curious about what learning to teach actually looks like day to day. The names of schools, students, and colleagues have been anonymised or replaced with initials throughout. Practicum-I was introduction to teaching and consisted of 13 reflections about setting oneself to look at how o teach and several visits to X School, Sukkur. In Practicum-II, lessons were taught in groups of three student teachers. One teacher conducted the lesson, while the other two observed and provided feedback. Here they are referred to as co-teacher H, and co-teacher N. The actual names of the teachers and schools have been replaced by letters. Practicum-III, taken in the sixth semester of the B.Ed. programme, required at least 10 full lessons taught at an assigned school, each with a lesson plan, a co-teacher’s observation sheet, and a written reflection, gathered together into a final reflective report and portfolio. Practicum-IV consisted of ten lessons at X School, Sukkur, teaching Grade VII and VIII. Practicum-V combined seven lessons, teaching grade VIII, with three micro-teaching lessons at the university, some delivered in pairs with a second student teacher. Note: The lesson plans, reflections, and reflective reports throughout this diary have been lightly edited and checked for grammatical accuracy for readability using Grammarly, ahead of publishing. description_en: Ten lessons, taught partly alone and partly in pairs, and a set of concrete recommendations for how the practicum itself could be better designed.
description_ur: دس اسباق، کچھ اکیلے اور کچھ جوڑی میں پڑھائے گئے، اور پریکٹیکم کے بہتر ڈیزائن کے لیے چند ٹھوس تجاویز۔
content: Over the 16 weeks of teaching practice, we were supposed to visit the school 12 to 14 times, or conduct micro-teaching at our university when we didn't go to the site. In the end, only 10 lesson plans, along with observation checklists and reflections on each lesson, needed to be submitted as an e-portfolio to the course supervisor to meet the course requirements. Throughout, the blend of classroom observations and post-lesson conferences was pivotal in making our teaching effective, understanding students' behaviour, and shaping our instructional strategies to engage them. We invested our energy in simplifying physics concepts through simple demonstrations. Selecting texts — excerpts from diaries, letters, and books — for lessons in Urdu and English also aimed to give students a sense of what kind of literature they should be reading. Telling students about the use of flowers during times of war sparked their interest while teaching history. To make mathematics, often considered the most boring subject, more engaging, we discussed its applications in daily life. Taking an interest in students' curiosities after class also showed that when a teacher appreciates them and provides relevant answers, students respect their teachers in turn. Throughout the bachelor's degree programme, there were several practicum courses, and this one marked the end of school visits to learn to teach and put into practice what we had learned. Each practicum taught us many things and improved our teaching, but this one was peculiar for several reasons that also made it enjoyable. First, we went to class in pairs, with one of us teaching and the other observing — a different experience from previous practicums, where cooperating teachers observed with little interest in or understanding of how prospective teachers should be observed. We observed each other and offered suggestions to improve our mishaps, considering both the circumstances and the theories we'd learned. The post-conference was also a novel experience, where we discussed the strengths and weaknesses of the lesson just taught, and shared difficulties with the course supervisor to explore possible solutions. Despite that, observation has its limitations. We were required to observe based on a provided checklist that doesn't account for a class's circumstances or a student teacher's philosophy. For instance, the checklist demands a variety of strategies within a lesson, but doing so in a class of 40 students creates nothing but havoc — we witnessed it firsthand. We held to a philosophy of engaging students in meaningful learning, without fixating on completing every planned activity on time, but the checklist would regard such lessons as ineffective and incomplete. Lesson plans should explicitly state a teacher's teaching philosophy, and be judged with classroom circumstances in mind. We also noticed, in observing classes and cooperating teachers, that the cooperating school ran on its own set of beliefs and rules — we're not sure if they're part of any school policy document, but we witnessed a couple of disruptive incidents that limited a teacher's authority. When someone interferes with a class's proceedings, whether the principal or a teacher, it's unacceptable to us. It disrupts the class, students lose attention, and it becomes very difficult to bring them back to the topic. It also amounts to treating a teacher as though they have no worth or value in the very room that is meant to be their playfield. Observations and post-conferences helped us identify the strengths and weaknesses of each lesson and prepare more effectively for the next. In one physics lesson, we used worksheets to assess whether students had learned a particular concept; distributing them in groups threw the whole lesson off. In the post-conference, we reflected that group work would be much harder in such a crowded class, so activities needed to be individual instead. That discussion guided the rest of our lessons and spared us further disruption. Some students also showed disruptive behaviour, and we had trouble completing lesson plans within 35 minutes, holding students' attention, and catering to individual needs. At times it felt like all the pedagogy, assessment methods, and classroom management techniques we'd learned were useless. To work through this, we approached our supervisor for feedback, reflected on our methods and plans, and developed lessons with students' interests in mind. Through constant feedback and support for one another, we refined our approach and adapted to students' needs. Changing sections from VIII-Daisy to Tulip also helped tremendously — the latter students may have received the Sindh Educational Foundation scholarship after a rigorous selection process, but they were also curious and serious about learning. In the end, observing lessons and taking part in post-conferences gave us practical field insight into teaching, learning, and what actually engages students. It made us realise how different the roles of a teacher and a prospective teacher really are — and how each role demands different strategies to face its own challenges. A prospective teacher can step out of a classroom when circumstances turn unfavourable; a teacher cannot. A teacher has to stay and manage the disruption. Whether it's right to change a class into a practice-teaching session at all remains, to us, an open question. We'd recommend planning the practicum to genuinely prepare prospective teachers for the role ahead, rather than treating it as a checklist of lessons to deliver, observations to sit through, reflections to write, and a report to summarise it all. Elementary teachers have to teach several subjects, so within a single teaching practice course, only one or two subjects should be the core focus, so prospective teachers can properly master them; planned well across all five teaching practice courses, there's ample time to eventually cover every subject. We'd also design the school visits in two phases: consecutive visits for a full week in the first half of the semester, then again in the second half — six lessons with observations and post-conference reflections happening back to back would do far more to connect one lesson to the next. In the gap between, prospective teachers would also get time to reflect and explore other options, and get more used to the actual rhythm and routine of a cooperating school. We believe the life of a prospective teacher, while practising, should resemble the real working life of a teacher and a school far more closely than it currently does. ← Previous: Practicum-V Reflection 10

description_en: Teaching angle construction from the floor of a U-shaped classroom, and connecting geometry to navigation and time dilation.
description_ur: یو کی شکل کی جماعت کے فرش سے زاویہ سازی کی تدریس، اور جیومیٹری کو راستہ تلاش کرنے اور زمانی تمدد سے جوڑنا۔
content: Imagine you are new to Karachi, in Saddar, and want to meet someone in Gulshan-e-Hadeed. You don't know the directions — what would you do then? This was the thought-provoking start to my visit on May 2, 2024. I had developed a lesson on constructing angles that are multiples of 15, using a compass and ruler. I changed the class seating arrangement, with the cooperating teacher's help, into a U shape. Instead of writing on the board, I used my rough copy to draw angles and diagrams while sitting on the floor, as there were around 20 students in the class. I then discussed the importance of angles in navigation and touched on time dilation. In the end, I asked students to draw various angles in their copies and explain, in their own words, the process of constructing an angle. It's almost unprecedented in our educational setup to thoroughly discuss the applications of a given topic in mathematics or physics with elementary-grade students. As a prospective teacher, I believe, and witnessed today, that students in grade seven or eight grasp concepts better when the application of what they're learning is discussed alongside it. Yes, students were already aware that an angle is the region between two rays with a common endpoint, and that a triangle has three angles. But they weren't able to visualise the use of angles in daily life — finding direction on land, at sea, or even in outer space. Secondly, when students are divided into small groups and concepts are taught in chunks, they're more likely to ask questions. To me, when students interrogate a topic, it means I've made it interesting to them, and they're willing to put in the effort to consciously learn something new. I'm counting the number of lessons, and with number nine, the practicum journey comes to an end. The students of the 8th-grade Daisy and Tulip sections may have learned something new in a novel way. Still, one or two lessons remain to be delivered as micro-teaching here at our university campus. After consulting with my teaching pair, I'll create a lesson on a physics topic suitable for undergraduate students — the B.Ed (Hons) programme's last teaching practice lesson. I hope it ends on a high note. Next: Practicum-V Lesson Plan 10 → ← Previous: Practicum-V Lesson Plan 9

description_en: On the 20,000-year history of counting, and why lecture-and-drill isn't enough to make mathematics feel like a joy rather than a wall.
description_ur: گنتی کی بیس ہزار سالہ تاریخ پر، اور کیوں محض لیکچر اور مشق ریاضی کو دیوار کے بجائے خوشی کا احساس دلانے کے لیے کافی نہیں۔
content: Mathematics is complex because we have a set of complex numbers. Is it, though? Out of curiosity, I tried to find the origin of mathematics. The first signs of it are often in the form of counting — "numbers" date back more than 20,000 years, recorded on bones, stones, and cave walls. Isn't it amazing that we count everything from the width of galaxies to the vibration of caesium atoms' electrons to set a second as a standard for measuring time? To begin teaching "number sets," I wrote a sequence of numbers on the whiteboard to determine how many numbers exist between two numbers, for the 8th-Tulip section on the 25th of April. Then I talked briefly about how counting numbers came into being. To address our growing needs and understand the complexity of the universe, we set out to discover more and more numbers by adding "0" to the front of a set of numbers, using "+" and "−" signs, and dividing one number by another. The addition of numbers was also discussed, and students were offered a reward for solving a challenging addition problem. Mathematics is aesthetic, and if one dwells on it, it becomes a joy of life. Otherwise, it's a problem with no solution in students' lives. The use of scientific calculators in 8th grade for simple two-digit division is of real concern to me as a teacher, and it's part of why the ASER 2023 report confirms that most primary school students across Pakistan perform poorly in mathematics. Teachers and schools aren't teaching concepts; they're training students to memorise mathematical rules. The classroom is a place of possibility, and students should be free to play with that principle to learn the core of mathematics. Secondly, today I felt that teaching mathematics purely through lecture and drill isn't enough to make students curious about drawing out patterns, substituting values, and inducing generalisations from previous patterns. Mathematics teaching needs to be interactive, as the observing teacher suggested, to engage students and make its abstract concepts easier to understand. After consulting with the cooperating teachers, I'll plan the next mathematics class — the 9th lesson of the practicum, and likely the last one, as students will soon have their final-term exams and, hopefully, all will be promoted to the next class. I've learned a lot from teaching in pairs and from the post-conference discussions, where we talked through the pros and cons of a lesson and how to tackle classroom and outside issues related to students' learning. description_en: Coining “the pedagogy of perfume” after hearing a student was barred from class over a scent a teacher disliked.
description_ur: 'خوشبو کا تدریسی فلسفہ' کی اصطلاح، یہ سن کر کہ ایک طالب علم کو محض اس خوشبو کی وجہ سے جماعت سے روک دیا گیا جو استاد کو ناپسند تھی۔
content: Imagine you are a teacher and one of your students is roaming outside the classroom. When you inquire, would it not be hilarious to hear that a teacher has not let a student sit in class because she did not like the perfume he was wearing? Unfortunately, this is a real incident. Laughing and wondering about it, I entered 8th-X to deliver my seventh lesson on April 18. I started by asking students to help me measure the dimensions of the whiteboard in centimetres and calculate the area in square centimetres. We reached a very large number, and I wondered how we could condense it or make it easier to handle. The students are sharp, and they quickly grasped the concept of scientific notation; I also discussed its rules. I tried to explain astronomical units and a light year, and compared the masses of protons and electrons to give a sense of how big and small the numbers we deal with in the world outside the classroom really are. Finally, I taught the students how to calculate someone's age in seconds, and to assess them, I asked them to write the previously calculated age (238,567,680 seconds) in standard form. Today's lesson was much more satisfying than the past few. One reason could be the change of sections, as I moved to another one. Secondly, I have good knowledge of "scientific notation" as a topic — I think content knowledge surpasses any pedagogy put into practice. Pedagogy is the method of how teachers teach, in theory and practice. Paulo Freire's pedagogy, for instance, is grounded in the belief that education is a political act, and that teachers and students should engage in a collaborative process of learning and emancipation. Here I am coining the term "pedagogy of perfume" — a phenomenon in which teachers use exclusionary disciplinary practices to remove a student from learning simply because they don't like that student. The pedagogy of perfume has negative consequences for a student's school performance, social development, and overall well-being. It can contribute to feelings of isolation, bitterness, and disengagement from school and learning. A teacher's role isn't just to teach; we need positive, constructive approaches to manage student behaviour and resolve conflict, putting aside personal likes and dislikes. In summary, the observer noted the value of establishing clear ground rules to minimise class disruption. Moving forward, I need to address these concerns promptly to create a more conducive learning environment and save instructional time by enhancing classroom management skills. I plan to collaborate with the cooperating teacher on the upcoming class to design a mathematics lesson aligned with the syllabus. description_en: A teacher pulls three students out mid-lesson without asking — and a hard look at what authority a prospective teacher actually has in someone else's classroom.
description_ur: ایک استاد سبق کے دوران بغیر پوچھے تین طلبہ کو باہر لے جاتا ہے — اور ایک مستقبل کے استاد کے پاس دوسرے کی جماعت میں دراصل کتنا اختیار ہوتا ہے، اس پر گہری نظر۔
content: Would it be right to say that the March 28 lesson simply adds one more to the target of ten lessons for the teaching practice course? No. Yes. Why am I counting the lessons? Is it because I am fed up with the interference of the school's teachers while I am teaching, or does the school culture simply not support my philosophy and pedagogy? Either way, it worries me as a prospective teacher, and I need to find an answer. Today, when I started my lesson, one of the school teachers came into the class, picked three students, and gave them a task to decorate the soft board at the back of the class, without informing me. I couldn't let it go, and I expressed my concern about that action. The teacher said, "It is very important, sir." I told her that learning is more important than an act that disturbs it. She then went out, took permission from the coordinator, and handed her grade 8 class, Tulip, to me. I am happy that the students in this section responded well and learned something from my lesson. Teaching is my vocation, and it will be an integral part of my life. For me, the teaching practice in the B.Ed (Hons) programme isn't just an opportunity to fine-tune instruction and deepen content knowledge, but a chance to keep an eye on the environment of the cooperating school, and to at least question the practices that get in the way of the learning process. It's not just about teaching and learning, but also about a teacher's subjectivity, shaped by the school's climate. Recalling today's class, which I'm now calling interference — where the teacher did what she thought was right and important — helped me understand why new instructors face resistance from veteran teachers in public schools. The established ones consider themselves right all the time and rarely let newcomers question how they've been running things. I think once a teacher is in a class, they should have the authority to prevent anyone from interfering with or distracting students, even for a single second, during the learning process. How can students focus on the lesson when another activity is happening in a corner of the room? Yes, it's important to respect a school's way of operating, but at the end of the day, any teacher, even one still practising, wants to improve the learning process. I consider today's lesson an improvement over past ones, as students showed interest in the manipulatives I used to present the topic's concepts. The observer suggested moving around the class more, so the student sitting at the back would also be engaged and encouraged. Keeping the supervisor's instructions in mind, I'll develop another science lesson for Thursday, though it's not yet clear whether we'll be going to the public school or teaching here at our university. description_en: Teaching the formation of the Muslim League while trying not to repeat a one-sided version of history from the author's own school days.
description_ur: مسلم لیگ کے قیام کی تدریس، اور اپنے اسکول کے زمانے کی یک طرفہ تاریخ کو دہرانے سے بچنے کی کوشش۔
content: Today, I tried to teach about the social and political factors that led to the formation of the All India Muslim League, as well as its aims and objectives. The 8th-Daisy students had quite good knowledge of the 1906 subcontinent, which helped me pace my lesson. I summarised the Muhammadan Educational Conference of December 1906, and the roles of Nawab Samiullah, Khan Bahadur, Nawab Waqar ul Mulk, and Syed Amir Ali in calling for a separate political party for Muslims. Sir Syed Ahmed had advised Muslims to stay away from politics until his death; still, the positive response to the Simla Delegation of 1906 regarding separate electorates, the establishment of Aligarh College as a university, and the partition of Bengal were among the causes that prompted Muslims to participate in politics. The new party aimed to promote loyalty among Muslims toward the British government, to protect Muslims' political interests, to present their needs and aspirations to the government, to remove misconceptions, and to foster cooperation with other communities. Teaching Pakistan Studies is always challenging, and it's not a neutral task. A good teacher has the responsibility to bring all perspectives of the various communities involved in an event into the discussion. In a religiously homogeneous class, one can teach a topic easily, but that isn't always the case. Presenting a single narrative may hurt students of other beliefs. Teaching this topic, "aims and objectives of AIML," made me remember my own 9th-class days, where my Pakistan Studies teacher portrayed Hindus of the subcontinent as trying to sabotage the interests of Muslims. But today in my class, there were Hindu students too, and as a teacher, I don't want to do the same and hurt the religious sentiments of my students. To some extent, I was successful in achieving my lesson's objective through the lecture method today. However, I still agree with the observer's suggestion that handouts should be provided in class, or in advance, to engage and enhance learning. Reading this reflection, it looks like I had a perfect lesson, but I found the class disengaged and disruptive. As prospective teachers, we go to the field once a week or once a fortnight, and students take this as an opportunity to have fun and relax from the burden of routine. We don't have marks to deduct or any power to take action beyond the 40-minute class. On the next visit, we have to start from scratch. In the future, it would help if the teaching practice were designed so teaching happens continuously for a week, followed by time to reflect, then another week of teaching. The supervisor has also emphasised integrating ICT into upcoming classes, but I'm unsure how to do that yet. Next, I'll be teaching a science topic after consulting the cooperating teacher. description_en: Teaching diary writing through Anne Frank, and wrestling with how to make reading and literature genuinely engaging in class.
description_ur: این فرینک کے ذریعے ڈائری نویسی کی تدریس، اور جماعت میں مطالعہ و ادب کو حقیقی معنوں میں دلچسپ بنانے کی جدوجہد۔
content: If Anne Frank had written this reflection in her Diary-Kitty, she might have written: "Years seem to have passed between my last visit and my March 7, 2024, visit, because so much has happened in between..." Anne is not here, but I did get help from her diary to teach 8th-Daisy about diary writing, which is part of their final-term syllabus. While preparing the lesson, I tried to use a personal diary entry, but unfortunately, I did not keep one — and now I think it is worth keeping at least a digital one. I also reached out to fellow prospective teachers to see if they could help, and one shared a diary entry, but it was not for grade VIII. In the lesson, I used a few entries from Anne Frank's diary, which she wrote from 14 June 1942 to 1 August 1944, at the peak of World War II. I distributed the entries in groups, and the students tried to understand what she had written. It caused a bit of disturbance, so I shifted to the lecture method — reading an entry and using the board to discuss the characteristics of diary writing. Finally, in groups, I asked the students why it is worth writing a diary. One thing that is clear from reflecting on today's lesson and the previous ones is that I love teaching using literature, whether in Urdu, physics, or English. The diary of Anne Frank has stood the test of time and is widely read and used to teach. The big question for me now is how to make the lesson engaging, since reading and making meaning from literature can be boring, at least for students in our context. We have not developed reading habits among students at either the school or university level. Giving a passage to read in class creates disturbance, but what else could be done? That is a cause for concern that needs resolving. Suggestions about aligning lesson objectives with assessment activities are worth focusing on, but what if the class doesn't engage with a certain set of predefined rules in the first place? Moving forward, I think lesson study could be a strategy, taking suggestions and planning lessons with my pair observer to address student disengagement. At the same time, it's tough to make the class a place to learn when we visit only once a week — we don't know what students are doing throughout the week or what they're up to in their lives. In the next class, I'll be teaching a topic from Pakistan Studies, after consulting the subject teacher. Next: Practicum-V Lesson Plan 5 → ← Previous: Practicum-V Lesson Plan 4

description_en: A second micro-teaching lesson on quantum physics, and the trade-off between covering a topic and keeping the whole class engaged.
description_ur: کوانٹم فزکس پر دوسرا مائیکرو ٹیچنگ سبق، اور موضوع مکمل کرنے اور پوری جماعت کو مصروف رکھنے کے درمیان توازن۔
content: In the second microteaching lesson today at our university, we taught a physics topic titled "quantum physics in our surroundings" to the students of B.Ed-VIII. We started our lesson with a short video explaining the concepts of the micro and macro worlds. Then we went on to draw a brief historical sketch of quantum physics, which began with the indivisible atoms of Democritus and ended with the discovery of the Higgs boson, a fundamental particle responsible for particle mass. To help students understand the importance of quantum physics in our daily lives, we illustrated this by asking students to smell burnt paper, a flower, and chewing gum, showing that even through our sense of smell, quantum physics is involved. For assessment, students were asked some questions, with explanations given to queries about the application of quantum physics, to bring the microteaching to an end. The purpose of our teaching was to help students understand the term ‘quantum physics’ through a simple example often overlooked. As students listened to this somewhat complicated term with patient equanimity, we felt that if concepts like this were explained by relating them to habitual affairs, we could make physics more interesting and easier to understand. However, while performing an activity in which we had to give students material to observe, we couldn't engage the whole class. The concern is that we failed to do so when we had an opportunity to engage more students. Apart from this, students could not remain on the same page, as our slow voice disengaged them now and then. Since midterms at the school are ending by the end of this week, our micro-teaching sessions have ended here for now. We will be going for teaching practice, teaching individually; the topics are not yet finalised, but we aim to teach from English and physics for grade 8. While delivering our lessons, we intend not to repeat the mistake of failing to engage the whole class, ensuring the activities are engaging. We will also try to speak louder, so students don't lose interest in the lesson due to difficulty hearing the teacher's voice from the side. description_en: A revised, paired lesson on letter writing — and a first experience of teaching alongside another student teacher.
description_ur: خط نویسی پر ایک نظرثانی شدہ، جوڑی میں پڑھایا گیا سبق — اور کسی دوسرے طالب علم استاد کے ساتھ مل کر پڑھانے کا پہلا تجربہ۔
content: نامہ بر تو ہی بتا تو نے تو دیکھے ہوں گے کیسے ہوتے ہیں وہ خط جن کے جواب آتے ہیں مضمون اردو اور سبق خطوط، وہ بھی جن کے جواب آتے ہیں اور وہ بھی جن کے جواب نہیں لکھے گئے، پر تھا۔ پچھلے ہفتے فیصلہ ہوا تھا کہ مورخہ 22 فروری بروز جمعرات کو جامعہ سکھر آئی بی اے میں ہی مائیکرو ٹیچنگ ہوگی، جس کے لیے ہمارے معلم اور نگران (سوپروائزر) نے اکیڈمک بلاک تھری، کلاس نمبر 502، ریاضی گروپ کے لیے مخصوص کر رکھا تھا۔ اس کلاس میں ہمارے علاوہ بی ایڈ-VIII کے 14 اور طلبہ موجود تھے جن کو "خطوط نویسی، کل اور آج کے دور میں" کے بارے میں ہم نے پڑھانے کی کوشش کی۔ ہمارے پاس کل 15 منٹ تھے۔ تدریسی عمل کی ابتدا ایک خط لکھنے کے ذاتی تجربے سے کی گئی۔ اس ذاتی تجربے کو افلاطون کے "ایک انسان کو مکمل کرنے والے اس کے دوسرے نصف" کی فلاسفی سے جوڑا گیا اور اس بات کا احساس ہوا کہ خطوط بھی لوگوں کو مکمل کرنے کا ذریعہ بن سکتے ہیں۔ اس کے بعد کچھ ذاتی تجربات، خط کی تاریخ اور خط کو کہاں کہاں استعمال کیا جاتا ہے اس کے بارے میں طلبہ کو آگاہ کیا۔ اس تدریسی عمل کے اگلے حصے میں ہم نے خط کو ادب کے طور پر اور اس کی اہمیت، خصوصاً خط کو درس و تدریس کے لیے استعمال کرنے کے پہلو کو اجاگر کیا۔ ہم نے مولانا ابوالکلام آزاد کی کتاب غبار خاطر سے، غالب کے خطوط میں سے ایک خط، اور کتاب صوفی کی دنیا میں سے چند جملے طلبہ سے پڑھائے، جس سے طلبہ کی دلچسپی میں اضافہ ہوا، اور آخر میں تشخیص کے لیے طلبہ سے دورِ جدید میں خط کی مختلف اشکال اور چند خط پڑھنے کے لیے کہا۔ ادب، خصوصاً خط کی اہمیت کو سمجھانے کے لیے 15 منٹ کا تدریسی عمل بہت کم ہے، لیکن اس موضوع کے لیے بھرپور تیاری اور طلبہ کی پرتجسس آنکھیں اس بات کا پتہ دے رہی تھیں کہ خطوط آج کل کے الیکٹرانک دور میں بھی بے بہا اہمیت کے حامل ہیں۔ لیکن ہمارا مشاہدہ کرنے والے دوستوں نے کہا کہ ہم اپنے سبق description_en: The final lesson of the practicum: time dilation, the twin paradox, and a perfect score to close things out.
description_ur: پریکٹیکم کا آخری سبق: زمانی تمدد، جڑواں تضاد، اور اختتام پر مکمل نمبروں کے ساتھ ایک شاندار اختتام۔
content: Have you ever thought about what time is? For some, it's an illusion; for some, an invention to sell clocks; but for some, it's an elephant, and we're blind, with very limited knowledge, throwing our observations at only the part of the elephant we have access to — only the part we can take hold of. I asked, "What is time for you?" and had students in B.Ed-VIII write their responses on Mentimeter to start the lesson on "time dilation" in physics. I put forward the twin paradox and the phenomenon of time dilation that explains it. With this, the second student teacher explained the frame of reference for observing objects at rest and in motion. He threw a ball to help students understand how speed, time, and distance are relative, and how the Lorentz factor proves it. He then shared the possibility of time travel for passengers on a fast-moving spacecraft as a dramatic application of time dilation, and closed the lesson there. The purpose of teaching time dilation was to familiarise student-teachers with one of the most complicated yet intriguing phenomena of relative motion, and to make students realise there is so much still to learn. If we want to really teach students physics, we must have knowledge that makes them wonder and opens up the possibility of imagining the unthinkable. The supervisor remarked, "Very good content knowledge, and you presented the topic confidently," with nothing noted in the checklist's suggestion section — certainly a boost to our confidence. Strong content knowledge is generally considered effective for instruction, but paired with students' genuine willingness to learn, it makes a lesson far more productive. We concluded this because we managed to engage students for most of the lesson, though their interest faded toward the end, perhaps because some were preparing to teach their own lesson right after ours. This was our last lesson, completing the ten-lesson practicum requirement. We're not sure whether there will be another, but this was the last one for us as a pair. We don't have to share what we'd teach next, or how we'd improve the next class. The only thing left to say is that we enjoyed learning to teach, and teaching to learn. Whatever we've learned, we'll carry forward as we keep teaching and learning in the days ahead. Next: Practicum-V: Reflective Report → ← Previous: Practicum-V Lesson Plan 10

description_en: Opening the practicum with a lesson on dreams, drawing on Freud, Iqbal, Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr.
description_ur: خوابوں کے سبق سے پریکٹیکم کا آغاز، فرائیڈ، اقبال، گاندھی اور مارٹن لوتھر کنگ جونیئر کے حوالوں کے ساتھ۔
content: 15 فروری بروز جمعرات کو میں ٹیچنگ پریکٹیکم-V کا پہلا درس و تدریسی عمل یعنی سبق پڑھانے کے لیے جماعت ہشتم، بوائز ڈیزی سیکشن میں موجود تھا۔ درسی منصوبے کے مطابق مجھے سبق "انوکھا خواب" پڑھانا تھا لیکن اس جانب آنے سے پہلے میں نے کلاس میں ڈاکٹر شاہد صدیقی کی کتاب "آدھے ادھورے خواب" کا خلاصہ پیش کیا اور یہ واضح کرنے کی کوشش کی کہ انسان دو قسم کے خواب دیکھتا ہے۔ بقول سگمنڈ فرائیڈ ایک خواب وہ ہوتے ہیں جو نیند یعنی غفلت میں دیکھتے ہیں۔ یہ خواب ہماری پوری نہ ہونے والی خواہشات کو چند تصاویر اور خاکے کی صورت دیتے ہیں، اور دوسرے وہ جو ہمیں نیند میں بھی جگائے رکھنے کی وجہ بنتے ہیں۔ جیسے کہ اس کتاب میں ڈاکٹر شاہد صدیقی اپنی عمر بھر کی کاوش، تعلیم کو بہتر بنانے اور اسے مزاحمت کا ایک ذریعہ سمجھتے ہیں، اور اس کتاب کے ذریعے وہ یہ خواب دوسروں تک منتقل کر رہے ہیں تاکہ وہ ایک دن حقیقت بنے۔ خیر کچھ خواب ادھورے ہی رہتے ہیں۔ بعد ازاں میں نے چند مشہور شخصیات، مثلاً علامہ محمد اقبال جنہوں نے برصغیر کے مسلمانوں کو پاکستان کا خواب دکھایا، کرم چند موہن داس گاندھی، جنہوں نے ہندوستان میں ذات پات اور عدم مساوات کی صدیوں سے چلی آ رہی روش کو ہمیشہ کے لئے ختم کرنے کی ٹھان لی تھی، اور مارٹن لوتھر کنگ جونیئر کی 1963 کی مشہور زمانہ تقریر "آئی ہیو آ ڈریم" اور اس خواب کا حوالہ دیا جس میں وہ امریکہ میں مقیم افریقی-امریکیوں کو ملک کے برابر کے شہری بنانے کی کوشش کر رہے تھے۔ اس تدریسی عمل کے دوران میں نے طلبہ سے ان کے خوابوں کو دریافت کرتے ہوئے تدریسی عمل کا حصہ بنایا اور خواب کی اہمیت پر بات چیت کی۔ میں نے آخر میں اس بات پر زور دیا کہ خواب کو حقیقت بنانے، اور دوسروں تک پہنچانے کے لیے تحریر اور پرچار کرنا ضروری ہے۔ اس پورے عمل کا مقصد یہ تھا کہ طلبہ خواب کی اہمیت کو جانیں اور اپنی زندگی میں کچھ ایسے خواب دیکھیں جن کے ذریعے وہ معاشرے میں موجود برائیوں کو دور کرنے کے لیے ایک طالب علم کی حیثیت سے سوچیں، اور اس بات کا اعادہ کریں کہ مستقبل قریب میں وہ ان کو دور کرنے کی کوشش کریں گے۔ بچوں کے چند سوالات سے میں یہ امید لگا سکتا ہوں کہ میرا یہ سبق کامیاب رہا۔ چونکہ کلاس میں بچے بہت کم موجود تھے تو مجھے کچھ زیادہ مشقت کرنے کی ضرورت نہیں پڑی، اگر کلاس کی تعداد پوری ہوتی تو شاید مجھے زیادہ دقت ہوتی اور میں اس سبق کو اس انداز میں نہیں پڑھا سکتا تھا۔ ایک طرح سے آج کا یہ تدریسی عمل میرے لیے بہت اہمیت کا حامل ہے۔ میں نے پہلی بار اردو پڑھانے کی کوشش کی، اور میری لکھائی اس قدر خراب تھی کہ میں نے وائٹ بورڈ پر زیادہ لکھنے سے اجتناب کیا۔ دوسری جانب میری ساتھی استانی کی رائے ہے کہ اس تدریسی عمل میں میری آواز کچھ دھیمی تھی۔ آنے والے جمعرات کو، گو کہ ہم سکول کا رخ نہیں کر رہے اور جامعہ میں ہی مائیکرو ٹیچنگ کرنے والے ہیں، تو میں اپنی ہم جماعت کے ساتھ تعاون کرتے ہوئے تدریسی خاکے کو تشکیل دوں گا اور کوشش رہے گی کہ بھرپور تیاری کے ساتھ اگلی کلاس میں آؤں۔ اور یہ امید رکھتا ہوں کہ اس تدریسی عمل میں جو کمی پیشی رہی ہیں ان کو دور کرتے ہوئے بورڈ کا زیادہ سے زیادہ استعمال کروں اور اپنی آواز کو بلند رکھتے ہوئے تدریسی عمل کو جاری رکھنے کی کوشش کروں۔ Next: Practicum-V Lesson Plan 2 → ← Previous: Practicum-V Lesson description_en: Constructing angles with a ruler and compass, framed around a question of navigation: how do you find your way in an unfamiliar city?

content: Grade VIII Duration 40 Minutes Subject Mathematics Class strength 40 Topic Construction of Angles 1. Students' Learning Outcomes Students will be able to: I. Construct angles using a ruler and compass. II. Demonstrate proficiency in geometric construction techniques. 2. Required Material Whiteboard, duster, markers or chalk, compass, ruler 3. Motivation Activity (5 Minutes) Imagine you are new in Karachi, Saddar and want to meet someone at Gulshan Hadeed. You don't know the directions, what would you do then? 4. Introductory Activity (10 minutes) Introduce the concept of angles in determining directions. Differentiate between Azimuths and Bearings, ways to measure directions and angles in land surveying and navigation using the figure. 1. 5. Activity 1: Construction of Angles (10 minutes) Demonstrate how to construct a specific angle (e.g., 60 degrees) using a scale and compass and teach the students to bisect an angle Guide students step-by-step to construct angles that are multiples of 15, i.e. 30, 45, 60, etc. 6. Assessment Activity (5 minutes) Provide each student with a different angle measure to construct independently. Observe their construction process and assess the accuracy of their angles. 7. description_en: Classifying numbers into sets — natural, whole, integer, rational, and irrational — and the idea of infinitely many numbers between any two.
description_ur: اعداد کی درجہ بندی — طبعی، صحیح، عدد صحیح، ناطق اور غیر ناطق — اور دو اعداد کے درمیان لامحدود اعداد کا تصور۔
content: Grade VIII Duration 40 Minutes Subject Mathematics Class strength 40 Topic Number Sets 1. Students' Learning Outcomes Students will be able to: I. Classify different types of numbers in sets(U). II. Demonstrate that there exist infinitely many numbers between two number sets (A) 2. Required Material Whiteboard, duster, markers or chalk. 3. Motivation Activity (5 Minutes) Begin with a quick game of "guess the number of numbers". Write down a series of numbers on the board. Ask, how many numbers are there between any two numbers? 4. Introductory Activity (15 minutes) Introduce the concept of number sets by explaining that numbers can be grouped into different categories based on their properties. Draw a Venn diagram on the board, labelling the circles with the following sets: Natural, Whole, Integers, Rational, and Irrational Numbers. Briefly explain each set and provide examples. 5. Activity 1 (10 minutes) Discuss and correct any misconceptions. Ask students to identify any patterns they notice between the different number sets. 6. Assessment Activity (5 minutes) Students will solve the problems individually, demonstrating their ability to classify and perform operations with number sets. 7. description_en: Measuring the whiteboard to arrive at a very large number, then using scientific notation to make it manageable.

content: Grade VIII Duration 40 Minutes Subject Science (physics) Class strength 40 Topic Standard Form/ Scientific Notation 1. Student's Learning Outcomes Students will be able to: I. Explain the need for Standard Form/ Scientific Notation (U). II. Utilise scientific notation in measurements (A). 2. Required Material Whiteboard, duster, markers or chalk. small square, measuring tape or ruler 3. Motivation Activity (6 Minutes) The teacher will measure the dimensions of the whiteboard with the help of the student. Calculate the area of the whiteboard and compare it with the area of a small square. 4. Universe's Distances and Sizes (10 minutes) Draw a large dot on the paper, labelling it "Earth." Explain the concept of astronomical units (AU) and light-years (LY) as units of measurement for distances in space. Discuss the immense distances between stars, galaxies, and other celestial bodies. 5. Scientific Notation Conversion (20 minutes) Explain the concept of Scientific Notation. Ask students to convert these numbers into scientific notation. Discuss and compare the sizes of the objects in scientific notation. 6. Assessment (5 Minutes) Challenge students to come up with their own examples of large numbers Have them convert these numbers into scientific notation. 7. Interpret the basics of sound amplification (U) II. Identify different sound amplification devices (A) 2. Required Material Whiteboard, markers, sound amplification devices, microphone, megaphone, loudspeaker 3. Motivation Activity (5 Minutes) Begin with a question: What is sound amplification, and how do sound amplification devices work? What are some examples of sound amplification devices? 4. Demonstration of Amplification (15 Minutes) Play a short audio clip or music at a low volume and ask the students if they can hear it clearly. Introducing and explaining the concept of sound amplification Discuss real-life scenarios where sound amplification devices are used (e.g., concerts, public speaking, hearing aids for individuals with hearing loss). 5. Group Discussion (10 Minutes) Hold a classroom discussion and ask the students to share examples of everyday situations where they encounter sound amplification devices. description_en: A 15-minute micro-teaching session using a flower, burnt paper, and chocolate to show quantum physics at work in an everyday sense of smell.
description_ur: پھول، جلا ہوا کاغذ اور چاکلیٹ کے ذریعے پندرہ منٹ کا مائیکرو ٹیچنگ سیشن، جو روزمرہ کی سونگھنے کی حس میں کوانٹم فزکس دکھاتا ہے۔

Analyse a few natural phenomena through the lens of quantum physics. 2. Required Material Board, chalk, duster, projector, speakers, a flower, a burnt paper and a chocolate 3. Motivational Activity (1 minute) The class would start with a short video showing some natural phenomena that can be explained using quantum physics. 4. Introductory Activity (5 minutes) Students will listen to the teacher. He/she will explain the concept of quantum physics by relating it to the video they watched earlier. 5. Quantum Effects in Our Surroundings (7 minutes) One of the teachers will hand students a flower, burnt paper and chocolate. The students will be asked to smell these things. Students will be asked, how come their tiny nose can smell such a multitude of distinct fragrances around them. Teacher will explain how quantum physics is at work whenever we smell something. 6. Assessment Activity (2 minutes) The teachers will ask some questions during teaching /at last, that require students to apply their understanding of quantum physics to explain a specific phenomenon. 7. description_en: A comprehensive reflective report on the Practicum-IV teaching experience at X School, Sukkur.
description_ur: ایکس اسکول، سکھر میں پریکٹیکم چہارم کے تدریسی تجربے پر ایک جامع تفکراتی رپورٹ۔
content: As a teacher, the first time I met the student outside the classroom, I was a stranger to them. The second time I met on the playground, I was an instructor. The next time I was their class fellow. Being with the students at the playgrounds and having small chats here and there throughout the practicum at X School, Sukkur, made this experience a bit different from the past ones. In this reflective report, I will discuss what I did during the ten visits to the school and what I have learned. There were a couple of experiences during the first few visits to the school that prompted me to go against the odds. The initial interactions with the school administration gave me goosebumps, as I, along with my colleagues, was instructed to follow the school's rules, like prisoners in a jail. Imagine you are at a place with more than 2,000 people who came to interact and learn from one another for 6 hours. You are advised to follow the rules that halt learning. Would teachers be able to work if they had no agency? Secondly, teachers are the drivers and facilitators of learning. What I had found was that teachers at this particular school were exhausted while checking student homework copies, developing lesson plans, and giving reports to school administration and parents about students' progress. This also made them stay in the staffroom throughout the school hours. And I doubt there was any concept of collegiality among teachers to share and learn from one another's experiences. It is a question to ask management: how would they take off some of the teachers' burden so they could spend more time with students, beyond the 40-minute class? I was there to learn, practice, and make mistakes. Throughout the ten visits, I tried to be among students from dawn to dusk. Teaching is my vocation, and I enjoy it. I played cricket with the boys of Eighth Daisy. The students were jubilant when I smashed a couple of boundaries in the very first match. On the football pitch, on occasions, students were dribbling the football around me like Messi. While the Seventh Rose girls were equally enthusiastic to play cricket and football, their access was limited to the basketball court. Spending time with students helped me tremendously in the classroom. Most of the time, we, the teachers, create a wall to exclude the real world from the classroom. This leads to boredom; students do not remain attentive to the topic under discussion, and the teaching becomes less relevant to their interests, which disrupts the class. I tried to connect teaching to their experiences by giving time at the start to discuss and express what happened when they were playing, especially when I was teaching the boy in the first half of the practicum. Moreover, I tried my level best to learn about their personal lives and how they are dealing with the unhealthy competition among themselves. In the second half, I taught grade seven girls, which was a novel experience for me, as I had never done so before. I used a VARK worksheet to collect data from the girls on their learning modes/styles during the very first interaction, and then developed the following lessons, analysing the data. One lesson was on listening, followed by reading, and the last two were on writing. Figure 1: Grade 7th Learning Style Data I had allowed the students to eat and move around in class if there was something important to share or discuss. Students always have a craving for snacks. When there are chips in the backpack, how will a student resist and focus on learning, which is all about paying attention and interaction? This slide changed the way I used to manage classroom decor and taught me that learning can take place while eating and moving in class. In this practicum, I tried to be a friend of the students, allowing myself to be with them. A teacher's work does not end after instructing for 40 minutes; rather, it continues in a continuous connection with them through thick and thin. By this, they feel free to share and learn. When I was about to leave on the last visit, one of my students, a girl, came to the bus door and said, "Sir, you are my favourite teacher." This is what I achieved at the end of this practicum. description_en: A free-writing lesson built from VARK data and a shared adventure story, on the second-last visit to X School.
description_ur: VARK ڈیٹا اور ایک مشترکہ ماجرائی کہانی سے تشکیل پانے والا آزاد تحریر کا سبق، ایکس اسکول کے دوسرے آخری وزٹ پر۔
content: November 29 was the day we visited X School, Sukkur, for the ninth time, which was supposed to be our second-last excursion of teaching practice. I developed a lesson to help students in 7th-Xappreciate the concept of free writing after analysing my students' VARK data. I started the lesson by instructing the students on a prompt story: I began with the exposition, then the students added whatever came to mind. Moving towards free writing, I wrote three words, "adventure, mystery and laughter," on the board. Still, I instructed them to put pen to paper for 10 minutes, forgetting about punctuation, spelling, sentence structure, and the use of heavy vocabulary in their writing. This lesson offered me some exciting insights as a prospective teacher. First of all, students love writing when there is no fear of being judged, graded or punished for writing a wrong sentence. The students were as busy as bees when they were writing, and no one was making any disturbance. A few students wrote a full page of a story, and others tried to write something of their own for the first time. Writing has always fascinated me as a student and teacher. I don't write much, which isn't a good thing, but when my students write, I feel complete. Secondly, I found that students value themselves when they are appreciated beyond academics and respect the teacher who helped them bring out the best in themselves. Today, as a male, I spent time in the break with the girls. That is, in itself, a taboo in this context, and to appreciate them is beyond imagination. When I brought their outside lives into class, they felt valued, and that is what teaching is all about. The way they played basketball and enjoyed the sport was something to be happy about. Interacting with students made me realise what bell hooks had said years back. An academy (school/classroom) is not a paradise where students want to be, but a teacher can create one where they can enjoy learning, which is missing in our schools. I wonder what a teacher could do to make students happy? The start could be to spend more and more time in breaks, and whenever a teacher finds an opportunity, instead of gossiping in the corners of staff rooms. description_en: Reflection on Lesson 7 - The Importance of Loud Reading
description_ur: ساتویں سبق پر تاثر — بلند آواز سے پڑھنے کی اہمیت۔
content: The continuum from one lesson to the next is what I like most about the 22nd November visit to X School, Sukkur. Last week, I engaged the students in a reading activity to find out their learning styles. Based on the collected data, I planned to go with reading aloud and listening drills this time. Before the class, I spoke with the coordinator and learned that it is against school policy to help prospective teachers provide the printouts. The coordinator gave me an undue favour by providing me with excerpts from the novel "Sophie's World," which turned out to be one of his favourite books. Fortunately, the photocopying machine was not working, and I got the prints from outside the school. Anyhow, it was concerning to me whether the actual teachers of the school needed some printed material, and if the machine is not working, it would halt the learning process. Many things made me feel happy about this lesson. Initiating the class by simply writing the title of "Sophie's World" on the board and inviting students to wonder about the story was an effective strategy. What I witnessed was that the students were curious and offered various answers. The diverse and large responses made the class interactive, where students not only demonstrated their prior knowledge but also indicated whether they were reading stories. The addition of an audio recording of the novel added a dynamic element to the lesson. The combination of auditory input with the simultaneous tasks of listening and reading engaged multiple senses. This multisensory approach not only catered to different learning styles in the classroom but also reinforced the content. And finally, the discussion on the importance of loud reading is a valuable addition to the lesson. The act of reading aloud, for example, encouraged students to make mistakes as they became fluent in the target language. This practice aids in comprehension and fosters a deeper understanding of the text. It's worth noting the importance of adapting teaching methods to accommodate various learning styles and to ensure a more inclusive and effective educational experience for all students. Moreover, it sets the foundation for a classroom culture that values oral expression and communication skills. As students become more comfortable with reading aloud, this strategy not only makes the lesson more enjoyable but also contributes to a holistic, effective learning experience. description_en: Teaching a packed girls' section for the first time, and learning how much adjustment a new classroom of 42 students demands.
description_ur: پہلی بار لڑکیوں کی بھری ہوئی جماعت کو پڑھانا، اور 42 طلبہ کی نئی جماعت کتنی مطابقت طلب کرتی ہے، یہ سیکھنا۔
content: It takes time for a teacher to adjust to new situations, both to teach and to learn from students. It became even more difficult when a teacher did not know the students' learning styles. Today, at X School, Sukkur, I was in the 7th-X section, packed with 42 female students. Not having experience teaching girls in previous practicums was a challenge for me. As usual, I stopped by the class during break time to interact with the students, but most were outside having lunch. I chatted with a few students and got to know them. The English lesson was based on a VARK reading activity that had students explore their preferred learning styles. While involving the students in the task of reading and completing the VARK worksheet, I was constantly thinking about how easy it would be for a teacher to teach a group of students with the same learning style. For example, a group of students love to read and discuss the characters of stories. It would be very effective, especially when learning a second language, as students would put the language into practice. In such a situation, teachers would not shout at students to pay attention to the board or to keep quiet. But unfortunately, as teachers, we do not consider this aspect: that students should be allowed and supported in learning the way they prefer. In Neil Fleming's 1987 VARK model, there are four learning styles/modes—first, the Visual learners, who like diagrams, pictures, slides, colours, and symbols. Second, the Aural/Auditory prefers stories and ideas to be discussed and explained out loud. Third, the Read/Write styles, where learners rely on handouts, notes, manuals, and workbooks. And finally, the Kinesthetic learning style: students love field trips, labs, real-life examples, the trial-and-error method, and problem-solving. It is not set in stone that students will have just one style. They could learn more than one style. During the class, I used the whiteboard to connect with visual learners, spoke and answered questions in English and Urdu simultaneously to focus on aural learners, and provided the reading and the worksheet to incorporate read/write learning styles into the learning process. But I could not think of any way to help kinesthetic learners; that means I am not able to facilitate their learning of something new. It is of great importance to me as a teacher to understand students' learning styles. Which style do they prefer to learn, or that excites them, so they will be fully engaged in learning when the teacher facilitates? Being aware of students' learning styles would enable a teacher to plan and incorporate activities into the class accordingly. description_en: Reflection on invigilating mid-term examinations.
description_ur: وسط مدتی امتحانات میں نگرانی پر ایک تاثر۔
content: The visit of 1st November to X School, Sukkur, was a bit different from the past visits, where we had to deliver a lesson and then reflect on our teaching and how we manage the class. This time there were mid term exams and we were supposed to invigilate one of the classes. The coordinator on my wish sent me and my colleague to the girls 7th-X section, where the students had already started to attempt their mathematics paper. Following the due procedure of not disturbing the students I silently entered the examination hall which looked very intense with an invigilator and 48 students in it. I think the addition of two as for invigilation kind of made the examination hall environment more severe for the students. The faces of the students were sad as it gave me the impression they were battling for their life or it was the mathematics paper that made it look so. I thought for a while what I could do to bring a smile to their faces and this thought took me to my matriculation and intermediate exams. At that time, the examiner tries to relax us by telling jokes or inspirational words at the start of the paper through the microphone. In between the break of paper-I and II at times we used to hear some poetry that clearly cheered up our faces. I wished I could have done that here but being for the first time on invigilation and unaware of the school examination rules refrain me from doing that. But somehow I end up writing "smile please" and drawing a happy face on the board. The second observation of mine is about the paper. The 100 marks paper was divided as paper-I and II, as objective based MCQs and subjective based CRQs and ERQs respectively. I doubt there is any chance of subjectivity in mathematics. Having a bit of knowledge about test development and evaluation made me analyze the paper. The paper-I was based on three chapters: set, algebra and coordinate geometry with 21, 16 and 13, MCQs respectively. This means there was unequal distribution of marks and importance was given to one or two chapters. The MCQs were mixed, and were not organized chapter wise making it more difficult to solve for the students. The paper-II was a bit better but there was no distinction between CRQs and ERQs as the questions were of the same type with the similar marks. There should be word problems in the ERQ section with higher marks as compared to CRQs. Finally, allocation of time for paper-I and II caught my attention. There were 50 minutes to attempt 50 MCQs of paper-I and an hour and ten minutes to attempt paper-II. At the end of the time for both the papers, students were pleading "sir one minute, sir one minute" as it usually happens in most of the examination halls. For a grade 7 student two hours are not enough to solve two papers of 100 marks. Hence, there is a need to pilot for time in order to set precise time for papers like mathematics which need time to calculate and check answers twice. When I talked to the respective teacher who set the paper for the class, she agreed with some of the highlighted points and gave a thumbs up to give a thought on this. For me the examination hall has always been a time to observe and enjoy the looks, peers make while attempting a paper. As a prospective teacher this experience and the serious faces of students made me realize we (students) are fearful of exams and it is a question mark on our education system. In an examination hall it is vital to help students to feel at ease so that they would attempt the exam by taking it as a daily routine practice.
