description_en: Questioning the banking model of education, and whether a lesson plan can double as a moment of guidance and counselling.
description_ur: تعلیم کے 'بینکنگ ماڈل' پر سوالات، اور کیا سبقی منصوبہ رہنمائی اور مشاورت کا لمحہ بھی بن سکتا ہے۔
content: The usual day-to-day lesson plan of our teaching practice seems outdated to me, as it focuses only on the banking model of education, where the more knowledgeable person (teacher) deposits a chunk of information in students' minds without creating knowledge or accounting for the factors that influence the learning process. In one of the counselling and guidance courses at my university, I came to understand the importance of counselling. So today I was questioning whether my students need any kind of counseling or a bit of help here and there that could help them to act as active learners and to be ready to learn something new. So before taking the class of 8th-Daisy, I sat with a couple of students and had a conversation in the break. I was looking at what could be the possible reasons that are barriers to the learning process of students. In that sense today was sort of another day for me at the field as I came to know about the psychology of students and the stresses they are having. Among the students whom I talked to today, one belongs to the minority Hindu community. The conversation with him revealed that the school management is not concerned about the religious festivities specially of the minority students. This particular student was worried about his upcoming exams from next week and not having a holiday before the Diwali celebration. My question is; would he be able to enjoy Diwali as he would spend his time preparing for exams? At the same time he was saying that when there is any religious event of the Muslim community there used to be holidays and the exam or events are arranged accordingly. This all was observed by an 8th grader. He was feeling segregated and excluded not only in the class but in the whole school and community. Secondly, there was another student who was counting only two true friends among the other 32 students in the class. These are just two examples and there would be other problems of students as well which need to be catered. I am sure that this unequal treatment is putting a lot of stress on him and such students. In a stressed situation it is next to impossible to pay attention to what is being taught in the classroom. In order to help the students to cope with such issues of psychological and socialization there is a need for a teacher to be a counselor. The teacher counselor would listen and help students to share their concerns and doubts in order to remain free from stress and to focus on what is going on in the classroom. Next: Practicum-IV Reflection 6 → ← Previous: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 5

description_en: A football-ground chat and a cricket match before class, and a reminder that no lesson plan survives contact with a real school day untouched.
description_ur: کلاس سے پہلے فٹبال گراؤنڈ پر گفتگو اور کرکٹ میچ، اور یہ یاد دہانی کہ کوئی سبقی منصوبہ حقیقی اسکول کے دن سے بے اثر نہیں نکلتا۔
content: I think things never go as we plan or want them to. It doesn't mean I didn't curate my lesson plan or enjoy teaching at X School, Sukkur, with the students of grade 8th. There is a break and a physical training (PT) period before science class. Today, during the break, I was at the football ground with the students for a while and observed their behaviour. While in the PT period, I was in the cemented area right behind the boys' section building and played cricket with the students for the entire period. Unfortunately, my team lost the five-over cricket match. Still, the particular experience of being with students both outside (playing with the students) and inside (carrying out the lesson plan) class forced me to question what kind of prospective teacher I am and how my teaching practice is shaping my identity. In the first place, I felt I was in pieces and questioned myself. Should I be a teacher who teaches what is in the test book, or a teacher who has the agency to go beyond the boundaries for students' learning? And certainly I have to answer this by myself. I witnessed joy and eagerness to perform better, and the students were giving their hundred per cent while playing, but once inside the class, they were not attentive. Is it because our prospective teachers' lesson plans focus only on the cognitive domain of knowledge acquisition? There is hardly any conscious effort in the affective and psychomotor domains, which makes learning boring. To overcome this boredom, students indulge in destructive activities, which ultimately leads to an unwillingness to learn. Secondly, there is a dire need to spend time with students. While playing and having small kachari (conversation) with the students, I came to know about their peer groups and their feelings. One particular student told me he has only two friends among 33 students, and the others never appreciate him playing or include him on their teams. This is a significant loss for the student's personal development, as he feels segregated. According to Erikson, a lack of encouragement can foster a sense of inferiority in children, ultimately leading them to doubt their abilities. Lastly, students need a bit of motivation to learn. Students can be motivated by small talk or a shabash (praise) for a small act within the class or during activities they do outside. But unfortunately, we don't give a damn about anything outside of achieving particular learning outcomes. As bell hooks rightly said, "the academy is not paradise, but learning is a place where paradise can be created". Moving ahead, it is of utmost importance for me to develop a lesson that focuses on all domains of Bloom's taxonomy to engage students mentally, physically, and emotionally in learning. Learning can only be joyful when the teacher praises and encourages the small acts in class and in other activities. Otherwise, students would be present in the classroom, but the outer world would capture their imaginations, and they would consume their energy learning nothing. Next: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 5 → ← Previous: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 4

description_en: Continuing the sound unit with amplitude and a group task, and a break-time discovery: nearly every student already has a private tutor.
description_ur: طول موج اور گروپ ٹاسک کے ساتھ آواز کے موضوع کا تسلسل، اور وقفے میں ایک دریافت: تقریباً ہر طالب علم پہلے سے ٹیوشن پڑھ رہا ہے۔
content: The third lesson was a continuation of the last lesson, where I taught about the loudness of sound, but this time it was about the relationship between amplitude and sound and how we measure it. There is a break before the science class, so I arrived about 20 minutes early and arranged the chairs for a group task. For some time, I mingled with students and discovered their interest in certain subjects. It was shocking to learn that almost every student had a tutor in an air-conditioned room at home, and I wondered why these students came to this school. When all the students entered the class, I let them make groups with their friends. The class was about to start when the supervising teacher came in and called a few students to the back to take a test they had missed last time. I should have stopped it from happening, but some unknown rationale overcame me, and I felt that the supervising teacher is bound by the school's strict rules, which require one to fulfil certain tasks, such as submitting test results and checking copies on time. Certain things were beyond my control, but others also caught my attention and were part of my teachings. The very first thing that went my way was the teaching method, which made me understand the importance of selecting a suitable method for teaching a particular topic. The selected lecture demonstration method, with the addition of group work for the topic, was better than last time. Science demands that phenomena/concepts be explained in ways students can see, touch, and imagine. The lecture-demonstration method helped me provide the basic information before the demonstration. I did not focus solely on telling the students what amplitude is; I involved the students in forming a wave using a thread and a tuning fork, and then had them explain its characteristics by reading the provided text in the books on their own. Secondly, I was surprised by the number of questions the students asked me during their group work. Previously, there were very few questions from the students, and I don't know why. But one possible reason could be whether a teacher appreciates questions and provides answers. At the same time, increasing the number of questions is related to the attention a teacher gives to each student because of smaller group sizes, as compared to the whole class. Lastly, assessment is something which I am worried about. I try to stay focused on the lesson topic and the SLOs. During lessons, I find that students lack certain knowledge, so I end up spending time on the day's topic. So sometimes I can't completely achieve my objectives, but most of the time I run out of time to assess the students. Today's lesson involved students in groups, and I believe they learned the concepts, but I don't have data to prove it. In the coming lessons, it will be challenging and pivotal to carry forward the good things from this lesson, such as choosing a better teaching method, appreciating every student's question, and responding to them healthily. And I believe there is a need to transgress to teach what I want the students to learn. Next: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 4 → ← Previous: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 3

description_en: A lesson on sound loudness taught with a mobile decibel app, and the small fixes a lesson plan reveals once you're watching yourself teach it.
description_ur: موبائل ڈیسیبل ایپ کی مدد سے بلندیٔ آواز کا سبق، اور وہ چھوٹی خامیاں جو خود کو پڑھاتے دیکھنے سے سامنے آتی ہیں۔
content: I had planned to teach about sound loudness and how to measure it using a mobile sound meter app. The observation sheet and the supervising teacher's comments are encouraging, as they indicate some improvement over the previous lesson. I maintained the board and wrote the lesson topic, but I still forgot to write the subtopic. I planned to assess the learning using a worksheet, but due to time constraints/mismanagement, I went to the students individually and in pairs to ask questions orally. To sum it all up, the class went smoothly, but there are a few observations/shortcomings that are important to address in the coming lessons. Foremost, I doubt the teaching method in this case, Inductive, was right for today's class. I started the lesson by generally asking how sound is produced and how it propagates from one place to another. In other words, I approached the topic from a general perspective, and students were already aware of it, which aligns with the teaching philosophy. But the teaching method should have been more of a demonstration or an experiential-based approach, as it engages most students and promotes hands-on learning. The availability of resources and teacher aids for experiments and demonstrations is to be answered, but science can't be learned orally. The second thing is more related to behaviour and how a teacher reacts to a particular situation and to students. In between, the students were changing their seats, exchanging water bottles, and making some noise. Later, I came across the fact that such disturbances are normal in the class, and students interrupt learning in other ways as well. There was a suggestion that I throw out students who were disrupting the class, but I restrained myself. Instead, I pretended to write the students' names to tell the coordinator, but in the end, I told the students I was acting. This might be helpful in the upcoming class; I think it helped me win the trust of a few annoying students. When I shared my experience of students making noise with a fellow prospective teacher, her response was "noise must have learning kaliya" (noise is necessary for learning). That is a perspective I need to understand, and I have to decide whether to give students the right to make noise and how much that should not affect learning. Lastly, this observation challenges the authority a teacher has over the students in the class until the end of the class. Today, during my lesson, a prefect and another boy disturbed my class three times. It is important to note that entering a class by anyone, even a coordinator, without the teacher's permission to give instructions and call out students breaks the rhythm, and it takes time to get back on track to teach again. Obviously, the prefect and the other boy were following the orders of other teachers and the management, who, I doubt, are not conscious of the disturbance they are making. If I get a chance to teach the same topic again, I would choose the demonstration method over the inductive, as it at least helps the student to see the miracles of science instead of listening. After the demonstration, I would divide the students into different groups and lead a discussion to engage every single student. Next: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 3 → ← Previous: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 2

description_en: A first real look at X School, Sukkur — testing its reputation and rules against the reality of managing thousands of students.
description_ur: ایکس اسکول، سکھر کا پہلا حقیقی مشاہدہ — اس کی شہرت اور اصولوں کو ہزاروں طلبہ کے انتظام کی حقیقت کے مقابل رکھنا۔
content: I have seen and witnessed the reputation of X School, Sukkur. For some, its popularity is linked to a well-known local university, as that university was founded in two classrooms of a public school. As a prospective teacher, I had kept all the theories and what education is all about. When I visited the School for the first time, the discussed rules and regulations forced me to frame a picture of the school that focused solely on managing thousands of students as followers. The second visit to the school, where I delivered the first lesson, went a bit better. Grade 8-Daisy has a class of 33 students, and there is plenty of space to move freely among them. I was a bit surprised when I completed the topic for days 5-6, six minutes before the allocated class time. The supervising teacher's remarks were also encouraging, and I ended up scoring 95 marks on the observation sheet. The supervising teacher commented that they would maintain the board and assess students' learning after the lesson. Between lessons, some students were not paying attention and were whispering and gossiping. I tried to engage them by going to them and asking them specific questions. When it comes to achieving the class objective, there is some doubt. Yes, I completed the lesson on time, but that doesn't mean I have transferred everything to their minds. It was my first interaction with the class. Without knowing their names, experiences, and learning styles, it was difficult to decide on a teaching method and strategy to apply. This lesson and interaction would help me to select the right approach in the upcoming classes. Next: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 2 → ← Previous: Practicum-IV Lesson Plan 1

description_en: An English lesson on the importance of loud reading, using Communicative Language Teaching with a constructivist approach.
description_ur: بلند آواز سے پڑھنے کی اہمیت پر انگریزی کا سبق، ابلاغی زبان کی تدریس اور تعمیری انداز میں۔
content: Grade VII Duration 40 Minutes Subject English Class strength 48 Topic The Importance of Loud Reading Philosophy: Constructivism    Approach: Student Centered    Method: Communicative Language Teaching 1. Students' Learning Outcomes Students will be able to: R U A A E C Total I. Explain at least two benefits of loud reading compared to silent reading - 50% - - - - 50% II. Demonstrate improved fluency and expression in their own reading - - 50% - - - 50% Total 100% R = remembering, U = understanding, A = applying, A = analysing, E = evaluating, C = creating 2. Pedagogy Learning Outcome Students would understand the benefits of loud reading and be able to apply this technique in their reading activities. 3. content: The Teaching Practice-III course of B.Ed-VI was the extension of Teaching Practice-I and II. In the last two practicums, we observed the different dimensions of the school, from gatekeeper to principal. We developed lesson plans and delivered lessons through co-teaching and micro-teaching. The Teaching Practice-III course required the following objectives to be achieved: At least ten lessons are to be conducted at the allocated school.The lesson plans need to be prepared following different models, e.g. KWL, 5E model, etc.An observation sheet has to be filled out by the co-teacher to give feedback.Reflections need to be written and submitted to the supervisor to highlight the learnings and loopholes of the lesson carried out.A summative reflective report has to be written and submitted to the supervisor.Finally, a hard portfolio that includes the lesson plans, observation sheets, reflections, and reflective report. The Teaching Practice-III course provided the opportunity to teach a full-fledged class at Government High School Number 01, Sukkur, for 10 weeks, starting on Feb 8, 2023. I taught mathematics and English to Section 7th-C in Urdu, and I also used English here and there, which some students found challenging to understand. In this reflective report, I discuss my experience of encountering several challenges and the lessons I learned from this teaching practice. Challenges Faced 1. Difficulty in Understanding Concepts I taught mathematics and English to grade 7. The students' mother tongue is Sindhi, and I couldn't speak it. However, the textbooks are in English. Using Urdu and English to deliver was a tough task. The language barrier made it difficult for some students to understand the concepts being taught. To address this, I tried to explain the concepts in the simplest terms, which helped some students better understand. I also provided additional time and explanations during break time to ensure that every student understood the concepts. 2. Individual Attention One of the main challenges I faced during the lesson was providing attention to individual students. With a large class size, it was difficult to ensure that every student understood the basic concepts. Moreover, many of the students struggled to comprehend the lesson when the language shifted from Urdu to English, which made it even more challenging for me to communicate effectively. During break time, I tried to talk to the students who did not respond in class and asked for their feedback. 3. Class Control and Engagement It was challenging to maintain class control and engage all students. Some students were not fully engaged and were disruptive at times, wanting to go to the washroom or to drink water, which took time to settle. This disrupted the lesson's flow and made it difficult to maintain the other students' attention. I tried to create an engaging lesson by incorporating hands-on learning and active learning techniques. Additionally, I tried to create a positive relationship with students to build a comfortable learning environment. However, some students still struggled to stay focused. Lessons Learned 1. Hands-on Learning and Time to Digest Information From this experience, I learned that hands-on learning/activities are necessary to teach students effectively. Active learning techniques, such as group discussions, problem-solving and role-playing, are effective in keeping students engaged and promoting a deeper understanding of the subject matter. Furthermore, I realised that students need time to process information before moving on to the next topic. Therefore, it's essential to allocate sufficient time for students to reflect on what they have learned and ask questions. Moreover, there should not be a significant gap between one lesson and the next to maintain continuity. 2. Role of a Teacher I also realised that the role of a teacher is not just to teach, but to give students hope and a reason to learn. There is always a lack of curiosity to learn from the student side. Students need positive reinforcement and encouragement to develop curiosity and a desire to learn. It's important to build a positive relationship with students and foster a safe, supportive learning environment. 3. Time Management and Lesson Planning During the lessons, I realised that students need time in class to process information before moving on to the next topic. At the same time, there should not be a large gap between one lesson and the next, but a teacher needs consistency in teaching methods and instructions to help students understand the concepts being taught. I also learned that it's impossible to implement a lesson plan in its entirety. Unexpected situations, such as disruptive behaviour or unexpected student questions, can arise and alter the original plan. Therefore, it's essential to be flexible and adaptable in teaching methods and instruction to cater to each student's individual needs. In conclusion, Teaching Practice III was a challenging experience. I tried to fulfil the course requirements by preparing lesson plans for each lesson, addressing feedback from the observation sheets, and writing a reflection on my teaching. Moreover, it provided me with some valuable insights into the teaching profession. I learned the importance of time management, lesson planning, active learning techniques and creating a positive relationship with students. Going forward, I am excited to continue learning and plan to use these insights to improve my teaching skills and become a more effective teacher. description_en: Why consistency in teaching matters, and why no lesson plan ever survives contact with a real classroom intact.

content: Reflection on Lesson X During the final visit to Government X School, Sukkur, on March 22, I observed the following points: A teacher needs consistency in teaching methods and instructions.It's impossible to implement a lesson plan completely. First, consistency is defined as the quality of being dependable, reliable and predictable. It involves acting consistently and stably and adhering to a set of standards or expectations over time. Consistency in teaching refers to the regular and reliable delivery of content, instructional methods and strategies, and to the regular assessment of students. When a teacher is consistent in his approach, students are better able to understand and engage with the material. It also helps to establish clear expectations for student behaviour and academic performance. When students understand what is expected of them, they are more likely to be motivated to learn and achieve their goals. However, consistency in teaching and learning does not mean using the same instructional methods for every student or every subject. Effective teaching involves using a range of strategies and methods to meet the needs of diverse learners. When students receive consistent instruction, they are more likely to understand and retain the material taught. Secondly, it is of utmost value to plan a lesson that provides a roadmap for a teacher on what to do in class and dedicates specific time to each activity. At the same time, it is true and difficult to implement a lesson plan completely. A teacher may encounter unexpected challenges or disruptions, such as student behaviour problems or technical issues. It is important for teachers to be flexible and adaptable in these situations and to adjust their lesson plans as needed. In addition, it is important to recognise that not all students learn at the same pace. Teachers may need to modify their instruction to accommodate different learning styles and abilities. This can involve providing additional support to struggling students, which takes up a lot of time. To sum up, for a teacher to make an impact on students' learning, there is a need for consistency in teaching methods and instruction. It helps to establish clear expectations and promotes engagement and motivation among students. At the same time, a teacher must be aware that a lesson never goes as planned and must be flexible and adaptable to meet the diverse needs of their students. description_en: Why gaps between lessons hurt retention and why students need time to process before moving on.

content: Reflection on Lessons VIII and IX During the ninth visit to Government High School No. 1, Sukkur, I observed three important aspects of teaching and learning: There should not be a greater gap between one lesson and the next.Students need time in class to process the information before moving on to the next topic.Active learning techniques are effective in keeping students engaged and promoting deeper understanding. Firstly, I noticed that the four-night gap between the last lesson and today's class necessitated revisiting the previous lesson. This gap gave students time to forget the previously taught information. It is important to review the previous lesson at the beginning of each class. This can help students recall the material and build on it, rather than starting from scratch every class. At the same time, revising a topic completely takes a lot of time. Secondly, I realised that students need time to process information before moving on to the next topic. It is essential to ensure that students have understood the material before moving on to a new lesson. Students learn differently, and some may need more time to understand the concepts. Therefore, it is important to encourage students to ask questions and provide them with extra time to reflect and process the information before moving on. By doing so, students will be more confident in their learning and better able to engage with the new material. Lastly, I observed that active learning techniques are effective in keeping students engaged and promoting deeper understanding. Incorporating activities such as group work, discussions, and debates can help students engage with the material, leading to a deeper understanding of the concepts. Active learning also makes the learning process more enjoyable and reduces the chance of boredom and disengagement. In addition, it allows students to learn from one another and promotes collaboration and teamwork, which are important skills for life beyond the classroom. In conclusion, teaching is a continuous learning process, and today's lesson helped me to recognise the importance of reviewing the previous lesson, providing students with adequate time to process information, and incorporating active learning techniques to keep students engaged and promote deeper understanding. As a teacher, I will strive to adopt these aspects into my teaching practices and provide my students with the best possible learning experience. content: Reflection on Lessons Six and Seven The important aspects of a class and teaching that caught my attention on the visit on March 1, 2023, to Government High School No. 1, Sukkur are: I haven't been able to create a positive relationship with students and a learning environment.The role of the teacher is not just to teach but to give hope and reason to students to learn.There is a lack of curiosity to learn from the student side. Firstly, after five interactions, I have been struggling to build a positive relationship with my students and foster a conducive learning environment, which has made me question how effective my teaching is. There could be several reasons for that. I might lack empathy or understanding for the students. Maybe I cannot communicate effectively with the students because I am using a third language to convey my message. But it is of utmost importance to have a positive relationship with students. According to Hamre & Pianta (2006), positive relationships with students can lead to improved academic performance, increased motivation and greater engagement in learning. Students who have supportive relationships with their teachers tend to feel safer and improve academically, and vice versa. Secondly, the students look aimless and hopeless about improving their current situation in terms of what they know. Therefore, the role of a teacher is not just to impart knowledge, but also to provide hope and inspire the students to learn. It's not enough to teach the content. One must also help students understand the relevance of what they are learning and how it can benefit them in the future. Therefore, I need to find ways to inspire and motivate my students to be more engaged in learning. Finally, I have noticed a lack of curiosity among my students to learn. This is concerning, as it may hinder their academic progress and personal development. I think building positive relationships with students and getting to know them better by engaging in brief conversations about their interests and discussing ideas and concepts beyond the classroom will make them more curious to ask questions and more active in class. In conclusion, as a teacher, I need to focus not only on imparting knowledge but also on creating a positive learning environment that fosters curiosity, motivation and eagerness to learn. I believe that by building positive relationships with my students and making learning relevant, I can help them achieve their full potential. Additionally, I faced challenges maintaining class control, as some students were not fully engaged and were disruptive at times, wanting to go to the washroom or drink water, which took time to settle. I did not achieve the class objectives because I focused on teaching the basics of the maths topic, which is required to move forward, and I ran out of time for the assessment. Teaching the first lesson of mathematics was difficult, but when I taught the second lesson in English, the students cooperated well. When I asked the students to recall the fundamentals of geometry, they were unable to produce any information. One of the main reasons students struggled was their limited prior knowledge of the topic. This was particularly evident in maths, where they had not yet fully grasped some of the fundamental principles of the topic I was teaching. Constructivism is a learning theory that emphasises the active role of the learner in constructing their own understanding and knowledge. Learners do not simply absorb information passively from the environment; instead, they actively construct their own knowledge by engaging with and making sense of their experiences. Learners bring their own prior knowledge and experiences to the learning process and build on this to construct new understandings. In addition, differences in language abilities and the fact that Urdu and English were their second and third languages made it difficult for some students to fully understand the subject. Finally, my lack of classroom management experience led to classroom disruptions, among various other reasons, including the fact that students at this age may be vulnerable to distraction and can be quickly bored if the lesson is not engaging enough. The classroom layout also posed a challenge: students were seated in rows and columns, with little space between them, making it difficult for me to move around and provide individual attention to each student. Moving forward, it is important to address these issues to ensure that all students can benefit from the lessons. To help students who need support with prior knowledge, I planned to incorporate more review activities and assessments at the beginning of each lesson. Additionally, I will continue to adapt my language and teaching strategies to help students who are still developing their language abilities. To address class control, I will consider implementing more engaging activities and group work to keep students interested and involved in the lesson. Overall, I plan to continue reflecting on my teaching practices and make adjustments to ensure that all students can learn and succeed. content: On Feb 8, 2023, I was in the field at Government X for the first teaching practice lesson of B.Ed-VI. I had planned to improve the 7th-grade students' speaking skills by giving them time to work in groups. Before my lesson, I was with my colleague, who was teaching General Science in Sindhi, and in the presence of their own science teacher, the students were responding. I started my lesson in Urdu and tried to shift towards the English medium. Next, I divided the class into pairs and groups of three students and instructed them to introduce themselves to each other in English. The class lasted 40 minutes, and at the end, some students came to the front of the class and tried their best to utter a few sentences in English. When I announced that I was going to teach English, some students were very eager to learn it, which was a good sign for me. Soon, I realised they were never exposed to speaking English, which became a challenge for me. The discussion activity was a chance for the students to prepare to start a conversation in English. Because the class was larger than 35, the activity did not go as planned. In between, there was a lot of noise, which created some disturbance. At the same time, I did not reach out to every student about what they were doing in groups or pairs because of the large number of students. As time was ticking, in a rush, I assessed the learning by allowing only a few students to come to the front of the class to share. Again, this raised doubts about whether all the students had learned anything. This was my very first experience teaching at a government school, and I was not familiar with the students, their level of understanding, or their English proficiency. The medium of instruction was also a barrier for me, as I tried to give instructions in Urdu to teach English, which is not their first language or medium of instruction. In the class, there was some noise, which is not bad when learning is taking place, but I think there was a lack of classroom management tactics. There is also a need to reflect on classroom management and devise a plan to run the upcoming lessons smoothly. This experience would help me in the upcoming lessons, as I am now aware of the ground realities. It is going to be tough for me to teach the students, especially English, but I have to work hard. description_en: Sitting in on exam day — two papers in one day
description_ur: امتحان کے دن کا مشاہدہ — ایک ہی دن میں دو پرچے۔
content: During our visit to the Government X School, Old Sukkur, last week, the school's administration informed us that classes would end this week and that the students would undergo exams to be promoted to the next class. This time, we went to the school not to teach but to observe how exams are conducted in government schools. When we arrived at school around 10 a.m., a paper was already underway, and we learned that another paper would follow after a short break once the current one was completed. The second paper of the day began shortly after. The assigned teacher in each classroom was responsible for providing answer sheets and question papers, and for recording student attendance. While the paper was in progress, the manager of this school and three others encountered a very stern lady, later identified as the Taluka Officer. She had come to observe the examination process and was annoyed by our presence at the school. I was taking a copy of the exam paper with the teacher's permission when I ran into the manager, who told me I couldn't have it. He reported this incident to our supervisor. After that, I tried to get involved in the examination process, but I felt like I was a hindrance, and the students seemed to be having some trouble because of my presence in the class. So I came out of the class and observed the old school building, built under British rule to teach women skills, which was later converted into a school. Tests and exams are assessment tools, and students are evaluated based on their performance on them. According to my observations, the exam being held at this school was not up to standard. For example, there were two papers for primary school students in one day — how do students prepare for two papers? This only adds pressure to the students. Second, there were no separate answer sheets and question papers for primary school students. Even university students are confused about how much to write on an answer sheet, so imagine how a student in grade two or three would decide how much to write. Finally, there was no light at school, and the temperature was approaching 50 degrees. In such conditions, it would be very difficult for a student to perform to their potential. Exams and tests help students improve. When taking an exam becomes merely a formality, it hurts the student. Exams should be conducted in a way that does not cause students to fear them, and the process should be as smooth as possible. content: This was our fourth visit to the X Government Primary School, Old Sukkur, and only one student from grade five was present when we arrived. According to the cooperative teacher, students are absent due to Ramadan and the extreme heat. It was co-teacher H's turn to deliver the lesson planned for grade 5, but things had changed for her like a nightmare when the cooperating teacher, after consulting with the head teacher, led us to a third-grade class instead. She began by telling the students about herself, and then each student introduced themselves. After asking the students about a table of single-digit numbers, the teacher began teaching counting numbers and some basic addition and subtraction. As we had to engage the students for three periods, the teacher eventually involved them in the poems by bringing them to the front of the class. This was a difficult situation for us to deal with. I wasn't the one taking the class, but I was there to observe as things unfolded. When you have a lesson plan for a higher grade and find yourself teaching a lower grade, things become extremely difficult. In such cases, you are unaware of the students' mental capacities, conceptual understanding, and almost everything else. The other challenge is deciding what to teach and how to teach it. The co-teacher did her best to address it by engaging the students, asking them questions about what they were learning, and then choosing a topic to teach. Such circumstances highlight the significance of a well-planned lesson. When a teacher has a lesson plan, they can carry out the lesson smoothly. A lesson plan specifies the lesson objectives and a variety of activities. A lesson plan tells a teacher what to teach, how to teach it, and to what extent — because you are aware of the students. Next: Practicum-II Reflection 5 → ← Previous: Practicum-II Lesson Plan 3

description_en: Observing and what it teaches to sit in the corner, take notes, and resist the urge to intervene.
description_ur: کونے میں بیٹھ کر نوٹس لینا اور مداخلت کی خواہش کو روکنا — مشاہدے سے کیا سیکھا۔
content: We returned to the field for the third time for co-teaching. This time, it was co-teacher N's turn to teach, and my job was to sit in the classroom corner and observe without disturbing the class. The co-teacher began the lesson by attempting to connect it to the previous lesson. The lesson was then immediately started and continued as planned. I was trying to keep one eye on the co-teacher and the other on the students and how they were responding to the teacher's instruction. Throughout the process, I took notes on the co-teacher's strengths and weaknesses. Following the class, I discussed my observations with the co-teacher and offered some suggestions for improvement. Sitting in a corner to observe students and a teacher may seem like an easy job. Still, it takes a lot of effort not to intervene and interrupt others' work, because when you are outside the frame, you get to see a different picture. I tried to suggest something to the co-teacher a few times, but my attempts were futile. Another thing I realised was how difficult it is for students to bear when a teacher is unprepared for the lesson, lacks content knowledge, or is draconian. Because the goal of a class is to educate students, learning will not occur if the environment is unsuitable. At the same time, it is extremely difficult to engage students in the ongoing discussion when the teacher lacks motivation or has a low voice. Being part of the class and observing the teaching process added valuable insights to my learning. It is crucial to have a voice that can be heard in every corner of the classroom so students can understand instructions clearly. At the same time, a teacher should have the content knowledge to answer every student's question; otherwise, students will become confused, leading to misconceptions. Next: Practicum-II Lesson Plan 3 → ← Previous: Practicum-II Lesson Plan 2

description_en: Delivering first lesson — low attendance, overloaded content, and what the co-teachers' feedback revealed.
description_ur: پہلا سبق پڑھانا — کم حاضری، مواد کی زیادتی، اور معاون اساتذہ کی رائے نے کیا ظاہر کیا۔
content: We visited the Government X School on March 3rd, 2022. In the classroom, the cooperating teacher was already in the middle of a math lesson. We waited for her to complete the lesson. It was my turn to deliver the lesson plan, but I was not fully prepared, as it always happens on the very first lesson. The class had 25 students, but only 14 attended. Initially, I tried to engage the students by inquiring about their daily routine. Then, while distributing some apples, I divided them into parts and asked different questions. This activity was planned to draw the students' attention to the topic "fractions." The class was over in the blink of an eye. During the lesson, the co-teachers observed my delivery and provided valuable feedback. The co-teachers identified weaknesses in my lesson delivery. Feedback was extremely beneficial in improving my teaching style and my interactions with students. As the co-teachers correctly pointed out, a teacher needs to know the students well, including their names, backgrounds, skills, learning styles, and areas where they need support. It was my first real experience as a teacher at a school. I was unaware of the aforementioned areas of the students' knowledge, which pushed me back from achieving the lesson's objectives, and I felt alienated in the class, which knew nothing about the subject. The second concerning aspect was that I overloaded the student with content knowledge without allowing adequate time for the student to digest the information. At the same time, I deviated from the main topic, which made the lesson difficult for the students. Finally, I was unable to properly assess the students to determine what they had learned. The identified weaknesses in my lesson delivery would be an opportunity for me to learn and improve. My energy, voice, and movement in class were all appropriate, but my performance in other areas was below average. As a result, this and future teaching and observation of co-teachers' lesson delivery will assist me. Next: Practicum-II Lesson Plan 2 → ← Previous: Practicum-II Lesson Plan 1

description_en: Practicum-II, a choice between an Urdu- and Sindhi-medium school, and planning towards co-teaching.
description_ur: پریکٹیکم دوم، اردو اور سندھی ذریعہ تعلیم اسکول کے درمیان انتخاب، اور مشترکہ تدریس کی منصوبہ بندی۔
content: Practicum-II was a step upon Practicum-I, which involved several visits to the X and Y Government School in Old Sukkur. During those visits, we observed and understood the roles of various aspects of the school, including the building, labs and laboratories, library, classrooms, management, teachers, the environment, and all staff who support the learning and teaching process. It also emphasises co-teaching and receiving feedback from co-teachers to further strengthen it. The Practicum supervisor taught us how to plan and implement a lesson in the first two sessions. Then we visited two schools selected by the Department of Education to plan lessons, learn about the students, and identify facilities that could be used during co-teaching. Both were primary schools, but one was Urdu-medium and the other was Sindhi-medium. The supervisor divided the student-teachers into groups based on whether they wanted to teach in an Urdu- or Sindhi-medium school. I end up at an Urdu-medium school with some other students. We went to the assigned grade 5th class, per the supervisor's instructions and with the permission of the school principal. For a while, I observed the teacher's teaching style and gained insight into her methods and students. During the break, I talked with the teacher about the students and the school. Finally, as a group, we decided to teach mathematics in the coming weeks and asked the teacher for a copy of the textbook. Visiting the school, I realised it would be very challenging to teach here. First, the school lacks necessities such as clean water and washrooms. Second, there is a scarcity of instructional aids used in the teaching and learning process. This is a huge challenge; now I must focus on no- or low-cost instructional materials to deliver a meaningful lesson. Yes, the circumstances are difficult, but that is the reality of education in our country. That's why one of my instructors used to say, "Teaching is not everyone's cup of tea.". Next: Practicum-II Lesson Plan 1 → ← Previous: Practicum-I: Reflective Report

description_en: Practicum-II final lesson plan: introducing grade 8 students to plotting irrational numbers.
description_ur: پریکٹیکم دوم کا آخری سبقی منصوبہ: جماعت ہشتم کے طلبہ کو غیر ناطق اعداد کی نقشہ بندی سے متعارف کروانا۔
content: Grade 8th Time 40 Minutes Subject Mathematics Class strength 25 Chapter Number Systems Topic Real Number line 1. General Objectives Students will be able to: develop mathematical curiosity when solving problems. become confident in using mathematics to analyse and solve problems both in school and in real-life situations. develop the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to pursue further studies in mathematics. 2. Specific Objective (SLOs) Students will be able to: plot an irrational number on the real number line. 3. Instructional Aids Board, chalks/board marker, textbook, compass, protector, scale, and pencil. 4. Motivational Activity The teacher will draw/show a unit right-angle triangle. Then for the length of hypotenuse will write the value of the irrational √2 = 1.41421 35623 73095 04880 16887 24209 69807 85696 71875 37694 80731 76679 73799... Next, the teacher will ask different questions from the student such as Can you guess what could this number be? Is it a rational number or irrational? Can you represent this number on the number line? To create interest in the students to learn something new and at the end of this questioning time, the teacher will announce today that we are going to learn to represent "an irrational number on the number line". 5. Previous Knowledge Students are aware of the number system, which contains rational and irrational numbers. At the same time, they also know about the Pythagoras theorem (c =√a²+b²) and constructing a perpendicular line using the compress or protector, because these topics are part of grades 6th and 7th mathematics. In an actual class, the teacher would try to teach the above topics if the students are unable to recall them. 6. Demonstration The teacher will teach the student by demonstrating how to represent an irrational, such as √2 and √5 on the number line using a scale, protector, and compass on the blackboard. 7. Assessment At the end, the teacher would give the number √5 students to plot on the number line to check whether the students have understood the concept or not. There was no reflection for Lesson Plans 4 and 5, as these were planned but not taught. Next: Practicum-III Lesson Plan 1 → ← Previous: Practicum-II Lesson Plan 4

description_en: A planned-but-untaught lesson introducing triangles
description_ur: مثلث کا تعارف کروانے کے لیے تیار کردہ سبق، جو پڑھایا نہ جا سکا۔
content: Grade 5th Time 40 Minutes Subject Mathematics Class strength 25 Chapter Geometry Topic Triangle and Its Types by sides 1. General Objectives Students will be able to: develop mathematical curiosity when solving problems. become confident in using mathematics to analyse and solve problems both in school and in real-life situations. develop the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to pursue further studies in mathematics. 2. Specific Objective (SLOs) Students will be able to: recall what a triangle is? differentiate between types by sides scalene, isosceles, and equilateral. locate some examples of triangles from daily. 3. Instructional Aids Blackboard, chalks, textbook, triangles made of charts and scale. 4. Motivational Activity To grab the attention of the students the teacher would ask a student to come on the board. Then the teacher will draw three random lines on the board and ask the student to draw a shape of his/her liking. If the student draws the triangle shape, then the teacher will ask the following questions. How many sides are in this shape? How many angles are in this shape? What is this shape called? Assessment The teacher would summarize the whole class by asking different questions from the students. Such as Tell me what a triangle is?
