description_en: A swapped class — stepping in for Co-teacher H's grade 2 lesson and improvising on the spot.
description_ur: ایک اچانک بدلی ہوئی کلاس — معاون استاد ایچ کی جماعت دوم کے سبق میں قدم رکھنا اور موقع پر بدلاؤ کرنا۔
content: Grade 5th Time 35 Minutes Subject Mathematics Class strength 25 Chapter 3 Fraction (کسور) Topic Basics of Fraction 1. General Objectives Students will be able to: develop mathematical curiosity when solving problems. become confident in using mathematics to analyse and solve problems both in school and in real-life situations. develop the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to pursue further studies in mathematics. 2. Specific Objectives (Students Learning Outcomes) Students will be able to: recall solving fractions with the same denominator. differentiate between fractions with the same and different denominators. solve the addition or subtraction of fractions with different denominators. 3. Materials & Resources Blackboard, different colour chalks, and textbook. 4. Greetings (4 Minutes) The teacher will greet the students and before going to the topic the teacher will inquire about their prior knowledge regarding solving fractions with the same denominator. The teacher will ask the students if they have any difficulty or confusion with the previous topic. After a short review of the previous lesson, the teacher will move on to the topic. 5. Introduction (2 Minutes) As the students are already familiar with the concept of fractions with different denominators so the teacher will move ahead with the topic. 6. Lesson (12 Minutes) The teacher will deliver the lesson with the help of examples given in the book on page number 33 example no 1. The teacher will explain the method of solving fractions with different denominators, such as taking LCM and then simply adding or subtracting them. There are numerous examples available in the book after their solution on the board the teacher will move to the exercise. As the exercise is quite lengthy, the questions which are more confusing will be solved on the board. In particular, questions involving three terms as given in the exercise part b and part d. 7. Discussion and Questions (14 Minutes) While solving questions on the board the teacher will ask the students verbally to tell her the procedure. Furthermore, the teacher will ask students who are willing to solve questions on the board. This will help the teacher to identify where students get confused or cannot solve questions. 8. Assessment The teacher will assess the students, and they will reflect upon their teaching method. The teacher with the assistance of a co-teacher will observe the students solving questions that will be an assessment. 9. Homework (3 minutes) The teacher will specify some questions from the exercise for homework. Note: Co-teacher H delivered the lesson. Feedback to Co-teacher H On what basis should I give you feedback, given that the intended lesson plan was not implemented in the respective class? The following is general feedback that highlights the sparkling areas and a few of the hollow ones. There were many positives to take away from today's class: The ability to make quick decisions. You did not even take a minute to decide what to do (tables and then addition) or how to teach grade two when the intended class, 5th, was wholly absent. Such ability is vital in teaching, as things never go as planned.There was scorching temperature, and you were full of energy. You were continuously interacting with students for one hour and forty-five minutes, excluding the poems and playtime, which certainly needs appreciation.Your voice was audible to the whole class.The other ability was to mingle with students. I guess they didn't feel any difficulty, since you were delivering a lecture for the first time.Bringing students to the board and asking them to solve questions, then using rewards to praise their performance, was a good strategy. I believe it has given tons of confidence to lots of students who were afraid to come forward. As the lesson was a spontaneous one, there's nothing to critique, but a few points that might help you strengthen your teaching further: There was limited movement on your part during the whole class — concentrated around the blackboard area. It's worth remembering to move around the whole class to have a glance.Initially, you started to teach about tables, then switched to addition. At this age, it might not be easy for grade two students to comprehend two topics and make connections between them.One more thing that could have been done was using the concepts of units, tens, and hundredths to further clarify the concept of carrying tens during addition.A short break after one hour or 45 minutes could have been appreciated, giving some time for the tiny brain to digest the information. I hope this feedback will help bring a little improvement. Next: Practicum-II Reflection 4 → ← Previous: Practicum-II Reflection 3

description_en: Co-teacher N takes the lead on adding fractions, lacks classroom control, and needs to work on volume and vocabulary.
description_ur: کسور کی جمع پر معاون استاد این کی قیادت میں سبق، جماعت پر کنٹرول کی کمی، اور آواز اور الفاظ پر مزید کام کی ضرورت۔
content: Grade 5th Time 30 Minutes Subject Mathematics Class strength 25 Chapter 3 Fraction (کسور) Topic Addition of Fraction 1. General Objectives Students will be able to: develop mathematical curiosity when solving problems. become confident in using mathematics to analyse and solve problems both in school and in real-life situations. develop the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to pursue further studies in mathematics. 2. Specific Objectives (Students Learning Outcomes) Students will be able to: Identify fractions having the same and different denominators. Add and subtract fractions with the same and different denominators. Solve questions given on page number 37 i.e. exercise 3.1. 3. Materials & Resources Blackboard, different colour chalks, textbook, different charts to represent fractions. 4. Introduction (5 Minutes) The teacher will greet the students and before going to the topic s/he will inquire about their daily chores and activities. Furthermore, the teacher will ask questions from the students to recall what they had studied about fractions in their last class. This activity will help them to connect their today's lesson with the previous one. A few questions the teacher will ask the students while greeting are as follows: How are you doing these days? How are you spending your Ramadan? Do you remember the fraction we studied in the last class? Can any of you tell us what is a fraction? 5. Lesson (15 Minutes) After recalling and checking the homework the teacher will start teaching about adding fractions of the same denominators. In the last class, we had already built their understanding and concept of fractions having the same denominators. As the students understand and can solve questions related to the same denominators, we will move to fractions having different denominators. 6. Discussion and Questions (8 Minutes) As the teacher explains the concept of addition and subtraction, now the students will be asked about their confusion. This time practice method will be used to explain the concepts. We have co-teachers present. They will assist students even when needed individually to solve questions of exercise 3.1 on page 37. 7. Assessment The teacher will assess the students and reflect upon their teaching method. The teacher with the assistance of a co-teacher will observe the students solving questions that will be an assessment. 8. Homework (2 minutes) The students will be assigned to solve part exercise 3.1. And they shall be instructed to mark the question they weren't able to solve. Note: Co-teacher N delivered the lesson. Feedback to Co-teacher N The overall experience of today's co-teaching was good, as you managed the class exceptionally well. Some of the positives are: The students were responding when you were asking different questions at the start and at the end of the lesson. There was little or no disturbance during the lesson, as there were appropriate moments in class, and your beady eye was on the balcony, watching every student.You tried to start the lesson where we left off last time, despite a gap of more than three weeks, by asking questions — very important in teaching, as the connection is vital to recall prior learning.The other good thing was the checking of homework. All the students who were present last time at least tried to complete it, and most of them succeeded.The last thing I like is that you kept the promise of the previous lesson, where Ms Humera had promised a reward to the students, by giving them some candies. When we keep our promises, people trust us — in this case, the student will trust the teacher, which is a must-have between the two. And certainly, there were a few things that could have been improved: Your voice was on the low side. You have to practise speaking a little louder. Yes, the number of students in this particular class was fewer, but what if there is a huge classroom with more than 30 students?The second thing which needs some improvement is the content knowledge. You prepared the lesson well, but you could put more effort into further strengthening your concepts about the topic "fractions." One thing you can do is give a demo in front of co-teachers or ask for clarifications from someone you like, so the loopholes in the lecture can be identified on time.Another minor thing that needs some attention is the correct use of mathematical language and symbols — like 1/2 and 1/4 being called half and a quarter, respectively, and using "=" instead of "//" for equality. The rationale is to enhance mathematical vocabulary; the wrong use of symbols by teachers would lead to the same by students, as they imitate whatever a teacher tells or presents to the class. I hope you take this feedback constructively and that it helps you improve in the future. Feedback to Co-teacher N by Co-teacher H The student-teacher performed really well. She managed the class and, despite its size and crowding, interacted with every student. She connected the previous lesson with the day's lesson. Some areas of improvement: Audibility: She wasn't audible to everyone, and she should ensure her words flow in a rhythmic pattern so students enjoy the lesson. While teaching, she should also create some form of drama.Mathematical terms: the student-teacher should use mathematical terms, particularly in Urdu, as it is the medium of communication and their course is taught in Urdu. Next: Practicum-II Reflection 3 → ← Previous: Practicum-II Reflection 2

description_en: Fractions lesson for grade 5, with feedback from both co-teachers on helping students who fall behind.
description_ur: جماعت پنجم کے لیے کسور کا سبق، اور پیچھے رہ جانے والے طلبہ کی مدد پر دونوں معاون اساتذہ کی رائے۔
content: Grade 5th Time 35 Minutes Subject Mathematics Class strength 25 Chapter Fraction (کسور) Topic Basics of Fraction 1. General Objectives Students will be able to: develop mathematical curiosity when solving problems. become confident in using mathematics to analyse and solve problems both in school and in real-life situations. develop the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to pursue further studies in mathematics. 2. Specific Objective (SLOs) Students will be able to: recall what a fraction is. differentiate between types as a proper, improper, and mixed fraction. develop the concept of equivalent fractions. solve the addition or subtraction of fractions with the same and different denominators. 3. Materials & Resources Blackboard, different colour chalks, textbook, different charts/sticky notes to represent fractions 4-5 apples, and a knife. 4. Preparedness (4 minutes) The teacher will greet the students and before going to the topic, he will inquire about their daily chores and activities. Furthermore, the teacher before the announcement of the topic will ask some questions related to fractions, which will be: How are you doing these days? Are you enthusiastic about the summers or sad? If I gave you an apple and asked you to cut it into four equal pieces and you eat one piece how much would be left? 5. Introduction (5 Minutes) As we ate an apple now let's see the topic which we are going to study today "fraction". Do you remember the fraction that you have previously studied? Can any of you tell us all what is a fraction? 6. Lecture (11 minutes) After knowing the prior knowledge of the students, the teacher will come to the main topic i.e addition and subtraction of fractions. The teacher will first explain the concept of numerator and denominator, then the teacher will solve examples on page number 33 of the textbook. After that, the teacher will solve and explain questions where the denominator will be the same and then another one with a different denominator. 7. Discussion and Questions (10 minutes) As the teacher explains the concept of addition and subtraction now the students will be asked about their confusion. This time practice method will be used to explain the concepts. The co-teacher will assist the teacher and will provide help to students even when needed individually to solve questions of exercise 3.1 on page number 37 of the textbook. 8. Assessment The teacher will provide sticky notes to the students to either represent, add or subtract a fraction during the class. The teacher with the assistance of a co-teacher will observe the students solving questions. 9. Homework The students will be assigned to solve part and b of exercise 3.1. And they will be instructed to mark the questions which they wouldn't be able to solve. Note: The lesson was delivered by the teacher. Feedback by Co-teacher H The student-teacher had a lesson plan. He delivered all the information which he had included in his lesson plan. However, certain areas need improvement. Some of them are as follows: Student Engagement: In primary classes, as it is important to create a sense of belonging in the classroom, a very simple strategy is naming the children while giving examples. As the topic was fractions, an example could be: Moiz has 1 banana and divides it among his friends, Amal, Ana, and Elif. This will involve the students in the example and create a sense of belonging in them.Consistent pace: The student-teacher gave a lot of examples to make the students understand the concept of fractions. However, the students of grade 5 seem already familiar with the concept, so fewer examples are actually required.For those students who couldn't grasp the information, many times the strategy of moving ahead works. It means that if they haven't understood the concept at the moment, they might understand a little later as the questions are solved. Too many examples can make things complex even for those who have already grasped the concept. If they still don't understand after solving the questions, a specific time shall be given to them to help them understand. Based on my analysis, these areas can be improved or were slightly weak and can be strengthened. Feedback by Co-teacher N The Teacher, while giving the lecture, needs to explain every aspect of the topic and avoid mixing up the concepts of like and unlike fractions. At first, he tried to explain the basic concepts of the numerator and denominator because most students did not understand the concept the teacher was trying to convey. And try to give more examples to convey the topic's concept clearly. The teacher's body language and energy delivery were good, and he tried to explain every detail. If some students did not understand, he would try to explain again and again, which was a good thing. Next: Practicum-II Reflection 2 → ← Previous: Practicum-II Reflection 1

description_en: Looking back on sixteen weeks of Practicum-I — what the visits taught me about schools, teaching, and myself.
description_ur: پریکٹیکم اول کے سولہ ہفتوں پر ایک نظر — ان وزٹس نے اسکولوں، تدریس اور خود میرے بارے میں کیا سکھایا۔
content: The third semester of B.Ed.-III started in October 2021. With other courses, Practicum-I was also part of the semester. The practicum course is unique in that it aims to provide prospective teachers with experience by exposing them to the school environment through weekly visits. It also has specific objectives, such as identifying connections between teaching theory and practice. The other rationales are: to collaborate with peers, cooperating teachers, school staff, and the practicum supervisor; and to develop professional relationships by observing elements of the school from the gatekeeper to the principal. Most of the lot was to invite, accept and utilise feedback from the cooperating teacher, supervisor and peers for learning. To achieve the objectives, the practicum was completed in 16 weeks. The supervisor allocated the first two weeks to discuss what the practicum is all about, what we (student teachers) are going to do in the coming weeks and to teach us how to write a good reflection. Then, for the following 10 weeks, we visited the Government X School in Old Sukkur, each time with an observation sheet listing a different objective to be achieved. Every visit added small chunks to my knowledge, and the supervisor asked every student to write a reflection to confirm whether they were learning and showing any signs of improvement. At the same time, the remaining three weeks were dedicated to reflecting on and presenting the learnings in three seminar presentations. And the last part of the lot was to write a reflective report summarising everything that happened in the semester. School is not just a building; it’s a place where pupils get an education. Education is only possible when a good environment is provided. A good environment includes a workforce comprising teachers and management. Still, good infrastructure is vital, including buildings with quality classrooms, labs, a library, a cafe, washrooms, a playing area, and every basic facility, from clean drinking water to first aid. By observing the Government X School in Old Sukkur from different perspectives, I learned about various elements of a school: how the different sections of the school are interlinked, and that chain is vital for a school to perform productively. Apart from this, the school visits and the process of reflecting enabled me to focus on certain areas, such as: The role of management in running a school smoothly.The use of available resources for the learning of students.How essential is the movement of a teacher in the classroom?What encourages a student to participate in the class?The importance of lesson planning.Which tactics can be used to check whether students are attentive or not? E.g. questioning, asking for opinions, suggestions and on-the-spot reflections, etc.The value of giving clear verbal instructions.Ensuring the involvement of all the students in class in the learning process.Why is it so handy to know the psyche of students?The vitality of policy documents for a school to deal with any matters of misconduct impartially.I went through the process of evaluating the performance of a teacher and found out that a teacher should have expertise in certain areas.I learnt about the responsibility of a teacher, where one should have an idea of what's going on in the life of a student, whether they are happy or bullied. In previous semesters, I learned about educational theories, how to manage a classroom, which teaching methods to implement, and whether a student- or teacher-centred classroom would be ideal for teaching in the 21st century. The practicum allowed me to test and verify theories of education in the field. It helped me tremendously by enabling me to compare the theories with what is happening in schools. Throughout the allocated weeks, I met with every possible person available at the school. At the end of the day, this experience of conversing and reflecting on the practicum's objectives, based on the observation sheet, helped me achieve them. When someone achieves their goals, they feel satisfied with the work they are doing, and that gives them the confidence to go beyond the set boundaries. In the first phase of five weeks, when things were shaky, unclear and incomprehensible, I felt the practicum was useless practice. The second five weeks were when I understood the rationale behind the practicum-I course, and the reasons became clear: one has to develop certain skills and qualities by observing the cooperating teachers and the school. So, from then on, I felt quite satisfied with the rest of the semester. I enjoyed sharing what I had come across with fellows and tried to learn from them as well. In reverse-chronological order, the practicum is a huge success for me, as I am meeting the set targets. The seminars helped me give deep thought to what I was doing throughout the school visit. Looking back, especially during the practicum's initial phase, I was going nowhere. It was the time when I thought this whole practicum course was a mere time pass and a useless thing. As time went on, things became clear, and I understood the objectives of the practicum. Presenting the experience to the whole class gave me the indication that I had observed the required things and learned from them. The whole semester was a tremendous opportunity to develop certain skills and to reveal some of the strengths and shortcomings in my personality. I realised I can remain focused on the task at hand and handle pressure. The other thing is, when responsibility is given to me, I believe I can offer my best by being cooperative and remaining impartial whenever there is a need of mine. My colleagues shared the areas of concern in my personality with me. It seemed strange to me to present the fact or opinion that I do not value or listen to others' opinions. On the other hand, I do not celebrate small achievements, but the accumulation of small memories and little successes leads to big events. The skills which I developed during my practicum are: A polite manner of communicating with professionals, peers and the people around you.Enhance my ability to question the things which are not moving on the track.Writing a better reflection than an average one.Improved presenting data and learnings in a few possible words during a presentation.The value of doing things on time, etc.Arranging data, saving and storing for later use in times of need, in online platforms like Google Drive, etc.A bit of my spoken and written English improved. There is always room for improvement, and as a prospective teacher, I believe one should be an all-rounder. Below are the areas in which I want to develop and improve: To improve my oral communication and further improve my writing.Making a good presentation using the available resources.The ability to work in a team and leadership skills. There is no use becoming a teacher who is not intrinsically motivated. One thing I believe was missing throughout the practicum was the motivation and passion that students and teachers would have developed by seeing the devotion of cooperating teachers to their profession of teaching at the respective school. The school which we visited was a place where anyone with high hopes would end up in deep despair. Next time, when I get a chance to visit the school, I will be looking to develop this by asking the cooperating teacher why they are teaching. The rest of the course's tactics and techniques were fine, as I went through a process of getting to know the school's dimensions. Next: Practicum-II Reflection 1 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 13

description_en: A lunch-break interview with a student named A.
description_ur: دوپہر کے وقفے میں طالب علم اے کے ساتھ ایک گفتگو۔
content: This was the seventh visit to the Government X school, Old Sukkur. This time, the task was to conduct an interview with a student. During the break, I asked A(a student) for his time. With full zeal and zest, A started his lunch time for my learning. In the interview, I asked about his background, his family and siblings, his early education, the language he spoke, the subject he liked most, his favourite teacher, his hobbies, and, finally, his friend circle. On the surface, A looked confident and happy with his life. According to him, this was the first time a teacher had shown interest in a student's life. Initially, in the interview, he was nervous, but then he responded well to the letter questions. He was confident talking about his background and family. When it was time to answer questions about the current school and teachers, he was a bit reluctant, and his face showed fear. He either limited himself to or excluded the question. This showed that the administration does not allow A or the school's students to speak out about how they feel. Next, when he was talking about his friends, he was trying to hide something. To me, it indicated that some of A's friends or acquaintances are not treating him well. Interviewing a student is one way to learn about a particular student. Once a teacher knows a student, they can build a good relationship with them. At the same time, knowing students helps a teacher plan the lesson according to their intellect and capacity to achieve the lesson's objective. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 10 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 8

description_en: How questions, tone, and verbal instructions shape whether students feel cared for — or singled out.
description_ur: سوالات، لہجہ اور زبانی ہدایات کس طرح طے کرتے ہیں کہ طلبہ خود کو خیال رکھا ہوا محسوس کریں یا الگ تھلگ۔
content: The goal of today's school visit was to observe how frequently a teacher uses the verbal involvement strategy in class and to understand its implications for the lesson. When I entered classroom 9th-A, the cooperation was a bit late, which gave me some time to quickly review the observation sheet for taking notes. When the teacher arrived, he greeted everyone and then asked a student from the front row for the mathematics textbook. Next, he started writing a question about logarithmic addition on the board. While solving that question, the cooperating teacher asked some students what the next step would be to ensure they remained on task. Now and then, the cooperating teacher asked several general and specific questions and gave oral instructions to engage the students. Questioning, giving instructions verbally, and engaging students in healthy conversation are essential parts of teaching. At the start of a lesson, asking students how they are doing gives the narrative that a teacher really cares about them, which is one of the basic needs of humans according to Malav's hierarchy of needs. Verbal involvement is vital and fruitful in preparing the class for a lesson by reminding them of the previous lecture and connecting it with the upcoming one. His clarity of instruction verbally motivates and provokes students to do better than they did on the previous task. Similarly, it encourages students to be active in the ongoing activity. On the other hand, when a teacher verbally engages with a student or a specific group, it gives the impression that the teacher is biased and that favouritism is at play. To be a good teacher, it is important to understand how vital it is to engage with the whole class verbally. Verbal involvement helps manage disruptive behaviour in class, encourages participation, and makes students more engaged in the ongoing activity. The teacher's healthy, unbiased verbal engagement with students makes students accountable. Hence, it is highly recommended that the teacher involve all students in class in oral communication. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 9 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 7

description_en: Tracking ten students through a maths class to see exactly when attention holds — and when it doesn't.
description_ur: ریاضی کی کلاس میں دس طلبہ کا جائزہ، یہ دیکھنے کے لیے کہ توجہ کب برقرار رہتی ہے اور کب ٹوٹ جاتی ہے۔
content: This was the fifth visit to the Government X School, Old Sukkur, to inspect and record when and why students pay attention in the classroom. It was mathematics class, as usual, according to the school's timetable. Following the instructions on the provided observation sheet, I excluded 10 students from the 31 present in the class and began monitoring their movements. The very first set of instructions from the cooperating teacher was to write down a solved question from the board and give it time. And most of the students under consideration for the observation paid close attention. In the next set of instructions, when the teacher was solving a question on the board, only 4 of 10 remained focused, while others were busy with various activities. In response to the third and final set of instructions, in which the teacher gave students a question to solve, only half of the students observed putting effort into solving it. The outcome of this observation is that the students were on task only during a single activity, in this case, writing. But the rest of the class, the activities, and the instructions went in vain, as they were not helpful or effective enough to keep students on task for a major portion of the lecture. When I shared the information with the cooperating teacher, he said, "Mathematics is a subject which needs practice and practice, so this habit of note-taking is helpful to them." At the same time, it is the teacher's responsibility to engage every student in the class by paying attention and communicating clearly. To maximise learning within the class, a teacher should have strategies to motivate and engage students for every set of instructions. To be a good teacher and engage students in a way that every second is productive, a teacher needs a plan and the ability to identify what is lacking. If I were the cooperating teacher, I could have used the formative assessment to check whether the students were on task. It is also important to keep an eye on every student with appropriate movement in the class. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 8 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 6

description_en: A teacher who hasn't planned a lesson in years.
description_ur: ایک استاد جس نے برسوں سے کوئی سبق منصوبہ نہیں بنایا۔
content: Observation to design a lesson plan was the objective of today's school visit. Till the time we reached the classroom, the cooperative teacher had already started the lesson. We observed the lesson, and the teacher was teaching a text from the English book about "Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai". He was using the blackboard to write the key points while reading the text aloud. In the next phase, the cooperative teacher asked students about Bhitai's background, name, early life and education, and finally about Bhitai's spiritual growth. A couple of students answered, repeating what was written in the provided textbook, like parrots. The homework was to write a short paragraph about one aspect of Bhitai's life. After the class, when we asked the cooperative teacher about his lesson plan for the topic, "to see how successful he has been in achieving the objective of the class." It was very shocking to hear the cooperative teacher say he had not been planning any lessons for the last several years. To answer the question, how do you teach a particular topic? He said, "I have enough experience to walk into a class and teach whatever the topic for the day is". At the same time, he emphasised the importance of the lesson plan for moving a lesson systematically. Knowing the importance of something and still doing nothing is a formidable crime. A lesson plan helps us focus on specific areas by allocating appropriate time to each segment. It helps us move at a learner-directed pace to achieve the lesson objective. At the beginning, it helps prepare students to learn something new, and at the end, it shows up and evaluates how much they have learned. If I had been the cooperating teacher, I would have planned my lesson. I would have divided the text into chunks and, accordingly, set some objectives. Students would be able to learn about Bhatai's early life and education. To obtain the objective, I would have used text outside the textbook. After the group discussion, the students would be asked to come forward and share what they have learned. This would help the teacher evaluate students' learning. Finally, a home task could be to read the poetry of Shah Abdul Latif Bhatai in the local language to connect this lesson to the upcoming lesson on Bhatai's life. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 7 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 5

description_en: An interview with a cooperating teacher and what that reveals about staying updated in teaching.
description_ur: ایک معاون استاد کے ساتھ انٹرویو، اور تدریس میں خود کو باخبر رکھنے کے بارے میں اس سے کیا معلوم ہوا۔
content: This time around, our task was to interview our cooperative teacher. After reviewing the observation sheet, my colleagues and I agreed on a few questions the teacher asked. From the cooperative teacher's reaction when we asked him about his previous time, he seemed to be trying to escape the interview. But, under continuous pressure, he reluctantly agreed to give some of his valuable time to our learning. The interview focused on classroom management. The questions were fairly simple, but the responses were fragmented, and only a handful of the information addressed the questions. There was this question: "What are your expectations from the students for a lesson and from the end of the academic year?" The straightforward goal was "to perform better", by which I suspect he was only focusing on the students to make them capable of just solving an exam paper. But what about skill development and character building? The other questions were related to the lesson plan, layout, managing behavioural problems, and students' participation in class. When the teacher answered the lesson question, he said, "It sounds good to plan your lesson, but in reality, it is of no use! I have enough experience to come to class and start teaching." In response to remaining questions, he blamed the previous teachers for not working on students' behaviour and the basics, which, he said, is causing problems for him and other teachers. The teacher did not mention straightforward strategies to address the problems. Based on the irritation with this particular cooperative teacher, I learned that teaching at this school has been stuck in the past. The teacher is using methods, strategies, or early rights to teach the 21st-century mobile phone generation. The profession of teaching demands that teachers adopt current tactics and teaching styles to manage students in the current era. This experience would be a reminder for me to be an updated teacher who never stops learning how to teach. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 6 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 4

description_en: Observing how a teacher moves in a classroom and what that movement does for engagement.
description_ur: استاد جماعت میں کیسے حرکت کرتا ہے، اور یہ حرکت طلبہ کی دلچسپی پر کیسے اثر ڈالتی ہے، اس کا مشاہدہ۔
content: On the 27th of October, we were in the field for another observation. This time, we aimed to observe a teacher's classroom movement and its impact on learning. When I entered class 9th-A, the teacher had already started the lesson for the day. I found a place at the back of the class and began observing the teacher. The time limit for observing the teacher's movement was about 20 minutes. I took my time observing and noting his movements. It was roughly 15 minutes into the period when the time was up. After the class, I asked the teacher about the importance of a teacher's movement in class. The seating arrangement and layout of any class are vital in determining whether it is student-centred or teacher-centred. Class 9th-A was in the form of a grid, where three columns and six rows were given to the class as a layout. There was enough between the columns to move freely, but the rows were close to one another, so there was no room for engagement. During the lecture, the teacher remained close to the board, but when he posed a question, he moved freely around the class. Often, the teacher checked their work by going to them. When I asked the teacher about the movement, he said, "It depends upon the layout of the class and what kind of subject you are teaching". To some extent, I also believe this, but whatever subject a teacher is teaching, it is important to be present throughout the class. So that no one would feel left out. By observing the teacher's movement, I realised how important it is for a teacher to move within a class. To be a good teacher, one must develop this habit to thrive in the profession. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 5 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 3

description_en: A first field visit to Government X School, Old Sukkur.
description_ur: گورنمنٹ ایکس اسکول، اولڈ سکھر کا پہلا فیلڈ وزٹ۔
content: For one final time before the school visit, we gathered in the smart classroom for Sir S's(practicum supervisor) last set of instructions. He helped us understand what to observe and how to observe it at school. Before leaving, one of the fellows collected the reflection of the previous class. It took almost 20 minutes to reach there, and it took a while to find the Government X School in old Sukkur. The principal welcomed us and joined us for a group picture. One of the school's helpers helped us navigate the school. Before the break, we visited and observed the library, science lab, and computer lab, and finally the administration office and the surrounding area of the school building. During the break, I spoke with students about the school. Right after the break, we were paired up and sent to observe the classroom. I ended up being inside X-A, where the instructor was teaching physics in Sindhi. I took notes about the class. When the period ended, we left for the campus. Overall, the school has all the necessary resources to run properly. The library has sufficient text and story books with enough space to accommodate a class, which would help to become self-learners. A science lab, possibly with all the required apparatus, from chemicals to microscopes, from models to specimens, could help the students to learn by doing. Computer labs, on the other hand, could be handy for connecting students with the vast knowledge of the world outside schools through the internet. In every institution, the administration serves as the nucleus, monitoring the school's progress. At the same time, it is responsible for providing and managing resources for teachers and students. In the coming days, as part of the observation at the school, I am keen to understand the school's functioning and whether the administration, teachers, principal, and students are supporting each other in the learning process. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 4 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 2

description_en: Setting rules for school visits, and why praising effort and listening to everyone takes time.
description_ur: اسکول وزٹس کے لیے اصول طے کرنا، اور کوشش کی تعریف اور ہر ایک کی بات سننے میں وقت کیوں لگتا ہے۔
content: The second practicum class of the 3rd semester was held on the 13th of October in the Smart classroom of the Knowledge Centre. All the students were busy giving the final touch to the reflection of the previous class when the teacher arrived. He greeted and placed the utmost importance on one aspect of morality in his opening remarks. He gave particular attention to acknowledging and appreciating an individual's efforts and contributions, particularly those of a teacher. Next, the teacher continued his lecture on writing a reflection, which he left in the last class. In the next section of the class, the teacher invited all the students to set some rules for the upcoming school visits. In this regard, students initially had to come up with five rules, each limited to 5 words. Next, it was to filter out the rules by avoiding negative phrases. Finally, we agreed on six rules with the instructor's help. The work of educational institutions is not only to teach a few words; their prime responsibility is to teach moral values, ultimately making good citizens. The teacher's emphasis on the quality of praising someone's effort was the class's takeaway. It is as simple to give respect as it is to take it. We have to appreciate individuals because it motivates them to do more and better next time. Secondly, I feel making rules is as difficult as obeying them. It took almost half of the class time for twenty-five students to agree on six rules. It takes time to form rules because we have to listen to everyone and weigh the pros and cons. A class which was half teacher-centred and half student-centred benefited both. The teacher achieved their aim on time, and students also enjoyed some freedom to participate in the learning process. Moving ahead, such an atmosphere would be suitable for achieving the course's objective. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 3 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 1

description_en: A final visit spent understanding bullying — its causes, forms, and a teacher's responsibility to notice it.
description_ur: آخری وزٹ، غنڈہ گردی (بلی اِنگ) کو سمجھنے کے لیے — اس کے اسباب، صورتیں، اور استاد کی ذمہ داری کہ وہ اسے پہچانے۔
content: On January 12, we conducted the last school visit at the Government X in Old Sukkur. The objective of being in the field was to understand the building, its causes, several of its forms, and to highlight it in the context of the school. The observation sheet provided helped to gather data from the school premises. Some define bullying as a notorious act where peers and seniors repeatedly or habitually use verbal or physical strength to harm others emotionally and physically. Bullying leads to a serious impact on the personality of both bully and bullied. In the long run, the bully becomes an oppressor, violating norms and laws, while the bullied faces severe psychological problems. The present bullying leads to isolation, depression, and low self-esteem, and at times leads to tampering. In some extreme cases, individuals think about taking their lives. Various factors lead to bullying, some are race, religion, social class, sexual orientation, appearance, physical or mental strength, size, age, gender, character, etc. Some of the types of bullying are verbal, physical, sexual and cyber, etc. Bullies either operate individually or in groups. Some people derive pleasure from inflicting suffering and humiliation on others. Sadism is a concept that describes a behaviour in which people derive satisfaction from making fun of others. At times, victims of bullying also become bullies for vengeance. Most bullying at the school level occurs in the classroom, during break time, and in the playing and recreational areas. Now, bullying is also being reported on social media and online platforms in the shape of ugly text and images. The tragedy of bullying is that it happens all the time around us, directly or indirectly, and to counter it, it needs huge efforts from individuals, from the roots, to take action to stop it in the first place. Allegedly, in the premises of a school, it is the prime responsibility of a teacher to know what is going on with a particular student. The pale faces of students at times indicate that someone is bullying and victimising them. A teacher should talk to students personally, assure them that they can be a source of comfort, and that the teacher will resolve the problem. Next: Practicum-I: Reflective Report → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 12

description_en: Scoring a cooperating teacher's performance — strong on content knowledge, weaker on planning and assessment.
description_ur: ایک معاون استاد کی کارکردگی کا جائزہ — مواد پر مضبوط گرفت، مگر منصوبہ بندی اور تشخیص میں کمزوری۔
content: Today's school visit was an observation of the lesson plan, during which I evaluated the cooperating teacher's performance. Keeping the objective in mind, I entered class 4th-A, where Sir A (a teacher)was teaching mathematics as usual. The provided observation sheet included several performance indicators, including lesson planning, subject competency, communication skills, classroom and time management, learning environment, interpersonal skills, and assessment. The aforementioned broader areas of performance induction were further divided into several subcategories. Mr A scored 68 points out of 100 on the provided rating scale, which is in the range of a good teacher. He performed well in several areas, but in lesson planning, classroom management, and assessment, he was not up to the mark. The cooperating teacher had a strong grasp of content knowledge, with over 20 years of experience. With updated lesson planning and innovative teaching methods, he can increase engagement and improve student participation in class. Being an effective teacher requires a grasp of several key areas, from lesson planning to delivering it with clear instructions and effective communication. At the same time, managing and evaluating students are important areas of the teaching process. Having expertise in only one domain, i.e. content knowledge, or a specific method of teaching, is of no use. Hence, it is the requirement of the teaching profession in the 21st century to compare all areas, from knowing the subject well to understanding students' nature. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 13 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 11

description_en: A school says it has a discipline policy, but no one can produce it in writing
description_ur: اسکول کا دعویٰ ہے کہ اس کے پاس ضابطہ اخلاق موجود ہے، مگر کوئی بھی اسے تحریری شکل میں پیش نہیں کر پاتا۔
content: The title of the observation sheet's discipline procedures and policies prompted me to find out whether the Government X School, Old Sukkur, has a discipline policy. The administration's standardisation answer was "Yes", but they were unable to provide any written documentation. This scenario raised several questions for me. How does a school deal with and prevent any disciplinary mishaps in the first place? And secondly, who has the absolute authority to decide the fate of those who misbehave? Next, I asked the cooperating teacher, who provides guidelines for managing discipline and other issues when there are no written policies. The cooperation teacher said, "The headmaster has the authority to take any action when such mishaps occur, and to a certain extent, inside the classroom, a teacher has the power to bring things under control." When a teacher has ultimate authority to make any decision, it sounds like a dictatorship in which students have no voice. Some teachers use punishments to curb unwanted behaviour, and others give warnings to bring naughty students on track. A lack of a clear discipline policy leads to partiality in actions and decisions, regardless of the severity of the misbehaviour; the teacher's mode of action determines the decision, so it is vital to have a clear policy. The cooperating teacher also highlighted the value of establishing classroom norms at the start of the academic year and reinforcing them throughout the year to avoid discipline problems. A discipline policy not only recommends actions to take against the same misdeeds but also prevents issues from arising in the first place. A teacher's role is to be a ray of light in the darkness for learners, and school policy should provide the path. When a teacher's thoughts align with a school's policy, it fosters confidence in the teacher. Then the teacher owns the school and students, which helps to take things into their own hands. At the same time, the students act in the circle of discipline and collaborate with the teacher and peers. Hence, a learning environment develops. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 12 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 10

description_en: Observing a student in maths class, a conversation about sketching, cricket, and group study.
description_ur: ریاضی کی کلاس میں ایک طالب علم کا مشاہدہ، اور خاکہ نگاری، کرکٹ اور گروپ اسٹڈی پر ایک گفتگو۔
content: The target of today's school visit was to observe a child. I selected A (a student) for the aforementioned objective. The moment I fixed my gaze on A, he was engaged in an activity with his friend next to him. He looked like a healthy child, with an average height and a sound body. Whenever the cooperating teacher gave instructions, he tried to listen and write at the same time, which I doubt he was giving the teacher partial attention. In between, A borrowed a notebook from a guy in front of him. At the last moment of the mathematics class, when the teacher asked a question, A asked his friend for help. 35 minutes were not sufficient for me to determine Arshad's strengths and talents. So, during the break, I interviewed him. After conversing with A, I developed a clear image of him. According to him, he would prefer group study to the traditional lecture method. In group learning with peers, there is no language barrier and no restriction on formal behaviour. A loves to sketch, but unfortunately, no one will appreciate him now. He also loves to play cricket and other outdoor sports. He is from a lower-middle-class background and studied in government schools where teachers didn't focus on individual students' skills and learning styles. Teaching is not only about uttering a few words on a topic in front of a crowd. It is also actually seeking to understand the nature and behaviour of a child. Understanding a child's nature helps a teacher identify strengths, talents, and weaknesses, and develop a teaching style that suits the student's learning style. At the same time, it helps a teacher plan a lesson tailored to a student's intellect, making it more productive. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 11 → ← Previous: Practicum-I Reflection 9

description_en: The first class of Practicum: a nervous room, a teacher full of energy, and a first lesson in how to write a reflection.
description_ur: پریکٹیکم کی پہلی کلاس: ایک گھبرایا ہوا کمرہ، توانائی سے بھرپور استاد، اور تاثر لکھنے کا پہلا سبق۔
content: In the very first class of Practicum, each Bed 3rd-semester student, as usual, felt uncomfortable before a new course. When the instructor entered the class, a few students rose from their seats in respect, and most remained seated. The teacher was full of energy, and he greeted with zeal and zest. Soon, students settled down, and for a split second, silence filled the classroom. Next, the teacher arranged a chair for himself at the Centre and began to introduce himself. Then it was time for the students to introduce themselves, and the instructor fired in some humorous questions, but the answers provoked the teacher to ask more. The very next moment, everyone was on their feet, laughing and screaming. As the intro section ended, the teacher used the projector to introduce the course and its outline. At the same time, the course outline demanded a lot of work ahead. Following that, the teacher highlighted the standards of teachers. Finally, the instructor taught how to write a reflection and assigned a reflection in class. Humorously introducing himself to the class eased the classroom's tense atmosphere. The teacher's energy told the story of his passion for his profession, which encouraged the students to adopt it as well. The introduction and outline of the course help students become familiar with the course and what they will be doing in the coming days. Learning how to write reflections enhances students' skills. The teacher's energy was at its peak even at the end of the class. This did not allow the students to engage in gossip or lose their attention. But at the same time, the humorous way the questions were asked made the class fun, which I would love to be part of. Next: Practicum-I Reflection 2 → ← Previous: About This Diary

description_en: On the teacher as gardener: facilitating a student's innate potential to learn, grow, and serve.
description_ur: استاد بطور مالی: طالب علم کی سیکھنے، بڑھنے اور خدمت کرنے کی فطری صلاحیت کو پروان چڑھانا۔
content: Imagine a rose plant cutting, buried two-thirds of it in a bed to grow a new one. In the bed, various flowers are already growing, probably not of the same colour and shape. The bed has all the necessary minerals, along with exposure to sunlight and a constant supply of water. There is also a gardener who, once in a while, only sees the cutting. With time, would the cutting grow into a plant, forming roots and shoots? It’s complicated to answer. Weeds would grow, preventing sunlight from reaching the cutting, and it would ultimately die out, losing its capacity to grow into a plant. In a second case, when a good gardener starts to nurture the cutting and the already-grown flower, facilitating the natural process by removing weeds and protecting it from being eaten by sheep or other animals. The rose cutting, one day, would fully grow into a plant and add its own beauty and fragrance, along with other flowers, to the garden. If the rose cutting is replaced by a child (student) and taught by a school, then there is always a need for a good teacher to facilitate the growth and learning. And this is what I believe and strive to be as a teacher: to get rid of the weeds and let the sunlight reach the plant so it can realise its innate potential. I believe that each child has the potential to learn, grow, and serve when provided with suitable environments and supported by a teacher. It is not always possible to appreciate, listen to, and care for the needs of each and every student in the classroom within 40 minutes. Therefore, it is vital to be available to the students. It’s healthy to remain among students and interact with them at playgrounds and other places, becoming their friend and classmate. This results in the removal of any unwanted barriers students might have to inquire and learn, and ends stereotypical thoughts. I am never in favour of being an authoritarian manager to maintain classroom decorum and deposit information in students, which Paulo Freire calls the banking model of education. Not allowing students to express themselves or pursue their interests, sticking to a single teaching method, and failing to engage students based on individual differences result in learning nothing new. Such practices create a living hell, and that is why Bell Hooks might have said this. “The academy is not paradise, but learning is a place where paradise can be created”. Teaching should be engaging and relevant to students’ interests. It is also the responsibility of teachers to develop awareness of what is happening in their surroundings, which should lead them to reflect and take action (Freireian praxis). A teacher must do a job to foster creativity. To achieve this aim, it’s effective to embrace students’ mistakes and create a learning environment that encourages them to take risks. Promoting collaborative learning helps students express, challenge, and refine their thought processes. By listening to peers, students also encounter new perspectives that broaden their horizons and deepen their understanding. I have the feeling that education should enable an individual to qualify, socialise, and develop subjectivity. According to Biesta (2010), qualification concerns the transmission and acquisition of knowledge, skills, and dispositions. It enables individuals to earn by doing something. Socialisation is about the thorough transmission of community knowledge, norms and values through interaction, which is thought to be part of the hidden curriculum. While subjectification refers to the process through which individuals become subjective beings, developing a sense of identity, agency and subjectivity. Conclusively, my teaching philosophy includes the engaged pedagogy of Bell Hooks and the emancipatory process of Paulo Freire, as I believe that contextual and engaging practices that transgress the language and authoritative ideologies in the classroom utilise the students’ lived realities to better facilitate learning. Moreover, the work of Gert Biesta plays a vital role in my teaching philosophy, as I wholeheartedly stand for the development of students’ skills, agency, and self-expression, so that their identity is formed, while also emphasising the role of socialisation and the development of strong social factors. This teaching philosophy was written in October 2023 as part of the Foundation of Education course. It has since been revised and is published here in its edited form.

description_en: A reflection on how reading, writing, and conversations shaped my identity, leading me to question the world around me.
description_ur: مطالعے، تحریر اور گفتگو نے میری شناخت کو کیسے تشکیل دیا اور مجھے اپنے ارد گرد کی دنیا پر سوال اٹھانے پر کیسے آمادہ کیا، اس پر ایک تحریر۔
content: The teaching literacy course has given me a whole new perspective on literacy, enabling me to interpret it in new ways. Literacy is an umbrella term that encompasses knowledge of practically everything, from oneself to others, from one’s family to strangers and from one’s well-being to inspiring individuals to revolt against oppressive powers. Hence, the acknowledged definition of literacy, the ability to read and write, has become more important for me than before. Reading provides awareness, food for thought, and highlights society’s wrongdoings. While writing is the most effective way to organise ideas, communicate with clarity, and express your perspective with confidence for greater impact. Every single activity begins somewhere; unfortunately, my memory does not help me recall how I started reading and writing. Formal schooling has taught me to memorise some letters in Urdu and English, which I suppose is not writing or reading, but a prerequisite. Until grade eight, I may have had positions in class, but I did not achieve literacy. Then there was a new school, a novel environment, and, in particular, a unique English teacher who made me realise why reading and writing are important. Often, the teacher would ask, “What are you reading nowadays?” If you come up with a book name, he would ask about a particular character and certain settings. It was impossible to tell a lie, as the teacher had been a student at the same school and had probably gone through all the novels and the library’s literature section. To be on the safe side, I started my first-ever book, “The Young Adventures and the Hollow Tree” by Enid Blyton. The children’s book was in hardcover, and it took me more than a month to finish the two hundred odd pages. The following year, another English teacher motivated and fostered a love of reading by saying that readers are leaders and by discussing leaders who were avid readers. Most of my classmates regularly borrow and lend books. A few of the mates used to read 40 to 50 pages an hour. I wish I had been able to read consistently to develop my language skills. Still, something is better than nothing. At the end of my college year, I had developed a sense of reading for pleasure, and that is still with me. When I started university, reading came to a halt, and I focused on writing. The English content courses, one and two, mainly focus on writing flawlessly by emphasising grammar and punctuation, but I got nowhere. The English content three-course again focused on reading, and soon I realised that without reading, writing cannot be improved. That is where I make some conscious efforts to read for writing and to write. Near the end of the course, I wrote a satire titled “The Right Way to Shit on…” which questioned the education system that individuals reach to universities, but still don’t develop the sense of how to use toilets. I presented the satire in class, and I am still proud of it today. It has taken a lot of time and effort. All the reading, writing, and other forms of literacy have helped shape the person I am today. Literacy has helped me to become more aware of my surroundings. Recently, I proposed improvements to the administrative and day-to-day operations of a department at my university. What I observed was revealing: those in positions of authority often feel threatened by people who raise legitimate concerns and point out specific problems. Rather than engaging with the substance of the issues, they respond by asking, “Who are you to question or tell us what to do?” and, at times, attempt to silence criticism through intimidation or by invoking authority. To me, this raises an important question about leadership, accountability, and literacy. If a person is educated and committed to the public good, should they remain silent in the face of clear problems, or do they have a responsibility to speak up? I continue to seek an answer to this dilemma: why is constructive criticism so often perceived as a threat rather than an opportunity for improvement? This literacy autobiography was written in December 2022 as part of the Teaching Literacy course. It has since been revised and is published here in its edited form.

content: SAJIDA: You let them talk over each other for ten minutes and call it a lesson. IMRAN: I call it an argument about a poem. That’s more than they did in your class today. SAJIDA: In my class today, every child could tell you what a metaphor is. IMRAN: Could they tell you why anyone would bother using one? SAJIDA: That comes later. First they need the tool. IMRAN: You keep handing out tools nobody’s asked for yet. I’d rather they wanted the hammer before I gave it to them. SAJIDA: And if they never want it? Some of them won’t, Imran. IMRAN: It’s not that your way is wrong. It’s that I watched a boy today figure out, on his own, why the ending of that story felt unfair. IMRAN: It’s not a story. It happened forty minutes ago. SAJIDA: (smiling despite herself) Fine. Next term, you teach the first two weeks your way. I’ll teach the two after that. content: Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy (1828-1910) believed that novels serve as tools for psychological education and reform, helping us understand one another, especially those who may seem unappealing at first glance. As the master of realistic fiction, he wrote acclaimed works such as “War and Peace,” “Anna Karenina,” and the novella “The Death of Ivan Ilyich,” which is considered one of his finest. His idea of nonviolent resistance, as expressed in “The Kingdom of God Is Within You,” has profoundly influenced 20th-century figures, including Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. In “The Three Questions,” part of the compilation “What Men Live By and Other Tales,” Tolstoy offers deep, insightful perspectives on various aspects of human life. One day, a king realised that the answers to three simple questions could lead to success in every task he undertook. To encourage participation, he announced a reward for the correct answers. People from all walks of life offered various responses: for “What is the right time to begin anything?” answers ranged from calendars and schedules to magicians. Similarly, responses to “Who are the right people to listen to and whom should we avoid?” varied widely. Some suggested listening to counsellors, doctors, and experts in their respective fields. Lastly, for “What are the most important things to do?”, no satisfactory answers were found. When no one received the reward, the king sought the wisdom of a hermit who lived simply in the wilderness. Upon encountering the hermit, the king repeated his questions, but the hermit was busy digging. By the afternoon, the king still had not received any answers. Just then, an injured man came running toward them. The king promptly tended to the man’s injuries. The following morning, the injured man apologised and revealed that he had intended to seek revenge against the king, which had led to his injury at the hands of his guards. The king forgave him and restored his property. As the king prepared to leave without answers, the hermit said, “You have already been answered. When I was digging yesterday, you helped me, and that was the most important time. I was the most important man, and doing good for me was the most important business. Then, when the injured man came, attending to him became the most important task, or else he could have died. He was the most important man at that moment, and what you did for him was the most important action.” Tolstoy firmly believed that literature and the arts could be used for psychological education and reform. The story of the three questions reflects his beliefs and thoughts. If we focus on living in the present, value those around us, and prioritise our actions, we can overcome many obstacles. Tolstoy summarises his argument: “Remember, there is only one time that is important—’ now.’ It is the most crucial time because it is the only time when we have any power. The most necessary person is the one you are with, as no one knows if they will ever have to engage with another. And the most important affair is to do good for that person because man was sent into this life for that purpose.” A century later, Paulo Coelho echoed these sentiments in “The Alchemist,” stating, “I don’t live in either my past or my future. I’m interested only in the present. If you can always concentrate on the present, you’ll be a happy man. Life will be a party for you, a grand festival.” By applying the philosophy of the three questions, we can lead lives free of hassle and depression. For instance, consider students in a class. If they occupy their minds with distractions outside class, such as social media and gossip, they learn little and end up blaming external factors for their struggles. Their priority should be the teacher, their classmates, and the topic at hand.

پر گفتگو کرنا چاہتا ہے تو ادارے اسے بات چیت کا موقع دینے کے بجائے خاموش کرانے کی کوشش کرتے ہیں؟ ایک ڈین ہو یا وائس چانسلر، اکثر سوال کو تجویز کے طور پر نہیں بلکہ نظم و ضبط کے مسئلے کے طور پر دیکھا جاتا ہے۔ پاکستان میں طلبہ یونینز پر پابندی صرف ایک انتظامی فیصلہ نہیں تھا۔ اس کے اثرات آج بھی جامعات کے ماحول میں محسوس کیے جا سکتے ہیں۔ جب طلبہ کی نمائندگی اور مباحثے کے راستے محدود ہو جائیں تو اختلافِ رائے بھی آہستہ آہستہ غیر مطلوب سمجھا جانے لگتا ہے۔ ایسے ماحول میں طالب علم سوال کرنے سے پہلے یہ سوچتا ہے کہ اس کی بات سنی جائے گی یا اسے خاموش کرایا جائے گا۔ شاید اسی لیے جب بھی میں نے کوئی تجویز دی، کسی پالیسی پر سوال اٹھایا یا طلبہ کے حقوق کی بات کی، تو اکثر جواب دلیل سے زیادہ اختیار کی زبان میں ملا۔ وقت کے ساتھ مجھے یہ احساس ہونے لگا ہے کہ مسئلہ میری تجویز نہیں، بلکہ ایک طالب علم کا سوال کرنا تھا۔ اب تک مختلف انتظامی عہدوں پر فائز افراد کو میں متعدد خط لکھ چکا ہوں۔ کبھی کبھی خیال آتا ہے کہ اگر ان خطوط، ان کے جوابات، اور ان سے جڑے واقعات کو یکجا کرکے قلم بند کیا جائے تو ہمارے تعلیمی اداروں کے مزاج، انتظامی رویّوں، اور سوال کرنے والے طلبہ کے ساتھ کیے جانے والے سلوک کی ایک دردناک داستان سامنے آئے۔ شاید تبدیلی کا آغاز ہمیشہ جواب سے نہیں، بلکہ ایک سوال سے ہوتا ہے۔ محترم استاد، description_en: A satire on education and educated.

content: Every day, people from all walks of life voice their concerns. Children want freedom from the beady eyes of their parents. Students are demanding their right to quality education and freedom of expression at educational institutions. And women blaming their male counterparts for being dominant and oppressors for ages, etc. At times, congregations discuss plans to break the shackles of oppression, and male treatment catches a lot of attention. But recently, I came across something peculiar, which gave me goosebumps. Toilets, yes, toilets, they were and are on strike. You would say I am insane. This is true, and before any disclosure, why they are on the roads, let me tell you about the caste and creed of toilets. Mostly, we have two types of toilets in this country. One is called the traditional, or Indian, and the other is known as the western, or English, toilet. The English consider themselves more advanced than the Indians. Well, both help us compute our daily chores, where we excrete the waste we take in as food. Time and again, toilets have been angry and have expressed their fury. But this time they are shouting, especially the English ones, about how wrong they have been used and want humans to compensate by taking concrete measures. They are also blaming us for being unethical by putting the full weight on the seat in a squatting position, and we don’t know the proper posture for sitting on the toilet seat or what to do after it’s been used. At times, they say that homo-sapiens don’t know how to shit properly. They think that we should be held accountable for our misdeeds. But wait a minute, English toilets are not blaming the illiterate ones or the ones who have never seen or used them in their life before. They have grudges and complaints about the behaviour of those who deem themselves educated, having studied, or currently studying at higher educational institutions. To an extent, there is no truth in pointing and blaming humans. We are the best of the creation of the creator, and we are above all. We treat all beings equally. And when we get an education, no one can compete with us in any sense. In primary and secondary education, we learn about ethics and etiquette. At higher secondary and university levels, we practice what we have learned without giving a damn thought to scoring a higher cumulative grade point average. Respecting others’ opinions, accepting things as they are, welcoming everyone and everything with a smile, and giving a hand to those in need are qualities we practise daily. Then, the blame for not knowing how to use a toilet is beyond comprehension. Well, if they are to blame, then we would see them in court. To make complicated things easier, the toilets had already issued a user manual. To use the English toilet, in particular, one has to lift the lid and sit on it like we used to sit on a chair. Bending forward by making an angle with the seat behind and raising the heels is also recommended for better performance. There is an option of seating adjustment attached to the lid; one can use it according to the bumper. When you are done with the most pressing thing of the moment, you have to use either toilet paper or water to clean the patchy area. At last, the user has to flip the lid back and press the button on the tank to flush the remains of what you have eaten hours before; it can be an unchewed, undigested bean, a conglomeration of hydrochloric acid and several of the gastric and intestinal juices. Toilets also claim to offer the best places where individuals can find peace of mind. Often claim that the best ideas originate on the toilet seat, where everyone feels free to think about anything. At times, we not only flash the waste but also the tamper, depression and ugly thoughts. Hence, it is a shame to disrespect the toilets which offer the best of their services to inhumane humans. Satire — any resemblance to specific institutions, policies, ministries, or ceremonies is, regrettably, not entirely coincidental.
